speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
that Bill C-74, an Act to amend the Constitution Act, 1867 and the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act to provide for certain matters in relation to the 1981 decennial census, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to be able to present this Bill to the House. On September 4, 1984, this Government was given a mandate to make positive changes in our key institutions of Government. These reforms focused on making Government more accountable to the governed for its actions. Parliament, in our democratic society, is the central institution of accountability, and this Government has taken a firm and very positive approach towards finding means by which the individual Member can play an enhanced role in the policy development process.
Very early in its mandate the Government acted on its conviction that the representatives of the people have a right to a significant role in policy development. It did so by placing a high priority on parliamentary reform. The Government took prompt action last spring to implement an important package of reforms to the rules and practices of the House. These reforms have gone a long way to giving committees of the House an important and independent role, which in turn goes a long way to enhancing the legislative and policy development role of the individual Member of Parliament.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that the Government has undertaken to consult widely before taking new directions in order to ensure that Canadians feel they have a part to play in the decision-making process. As part of this consultation process the Government published a White Paper on redistribution which I laid on the Table on June 11, 1985, and which was referred for consideration by the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections. After careful consideration of the proposed amendments to the Constitution Act of 1867 and the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act, the committee
reported favourably on the subject matter of the proposed draft Bill contained in the White Paper.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to thank members of the Committee for their invaluable assistance in preparing this new legislation.

I would like to remind the House of some of the key features of this Bill. The first and most significant is the change in the formula for calculating the number of seats for each province. The alteration will mean that the size of the House will grow more slowly than would have been the case if the current legislation were to be left unaltered. The House will know that under the present formula there would be 310 Members in this House after the implementation of the reports of the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Commission. Instead, the legislation we have before us now would see the House grow to only 289 seats after a new redistribution which can be in place before the next general election if we act with expedition now.
When the White Paper was published, most of the media attention focused on the direct costs of adding new Members to this House. I do not wish to dwell on this aspect but I will say in passing that we can anticipate a considerable saving by implementing the Bill now before us. Increasing the number of Members in the House will also necessitate increased expenditures on support personnel for Members, security and protective services, maintenance services, messenger and cafeteria services, and outlays for office renovation and accommodation. I think it is important that Parliament itself make cost effective decisions. The fiscally responsible approach to redistribution set out in the White Paper on redistribution may explain much of the very positive media reaction which was generated.
In the first redistribution after the passage of this Bill, even allowing for the cost of the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Commissions, the saving will be in the order of $1 million in the first year alone based on 1984 figures. While cost should not be the sole determining factor in deciding whether the House ought to proceed with this legislation, the House cannot ignore its importance to the taxpayers of this country. If unaltered, the House would increase in size over the coming two decades to 343 Members after the decennial census of 1991, and to a projected 369 seats after the decennial census of the year 2001. Such projected dramatic increases in the size of the House have provoked many Members of the House to consider whether such growth is desirable, and to wonder if it is possible to design a better formula which would be consistent with the needs of the electorate, but would not

Representation Act, 1985
promote such radical growth in the number of Members. It is my view that a major improvement is possible.
In developing a new formula to govern the redistribution process there are a number of matters which must be borne in mind. First, one must assess the impact of increased membership on the character and quality of the House. Mr. Speaker, I am concerned that we will lose an important sense of collegial-ity if the House becomes much larger, and that private Members will have diminished opportunities to become involved in the legislative and policy development process. Participation in debates on the floor of the House and meaningful involvement in committee work are directly related to the number of Members who are in competition for the limited time available in these forums. House time is scarce and opportunities to participate in debate are limited.
You will be aware, Mr. Speaker, of the increasingly important role being given to the standing committees by the House. The reforms brought in with all Party consent in June have radically altered the significance of membership on committees. This enhanced role has made it certain that there will be greater competition for participation on committees. In addition, there has been a trend toward smaller committees since the reforms of 1982, and still smaller committees have been recommended in the third report of the Special Committee on Reform of the House of Commons. If accepted, implementation of this recommendation would mean that members of committees will be given even greater opportunity for meaningful contributions to the policy development process and they will be given the chance to develop some real expertise in the policy areas covered by the committees of which they are permanent members. However, it is obvious that, if at the same time the House is permitted to grow in the explosive manner contemplated by the legislation now in force, there will be greater competition for membership on these smaller committees and, as a result, fewer private Members will have the opportunity to play a significant role in policy development.
The House will appreciate that with the significant reforms the Government has undertaken since coming to office, Parliament is a very different institution today than it was a short 12 months ago. Mr. Speaker, I think that the improved quality of Parliament's contribution to the over-all development and implementation of policy argues in itself for an enhanced quality of representation instead of a rapidly expanding quantity of representation. In my view, no evidence exists that a larger House of Commons would be a better House. I must state that the only way to improve the quality of the House is by courageously undertaking a program of reform to make the institution the best that it can be.
You may recall, as I do, that not too many years ago Members had no staff, no private offices nor constituency offices, and few, if any, of the amenities that Members of this House have come to take for granted. In recent years the capacity and quality of service to constituents by Members of Parliament has increased steadily as sophisticated equipment,
energetic and dedicated staff, constituency offices, householder mailings, and greatly enhanced transportation facilities have permitted Members to have an immediacy of contact with their constituents such as they have never known before. In the near future rapid technological developments, such as the use of computers and electronic mail, will allow individual Members of Parliament to communicate more and more effectively with an increasing number of constituents. For these reasons, 1 concluded that it would be unwise to allow a dramatic increase in the size of the House much beyond its present level. This is the First consideration upon which the proposed formula is based.
The second factor which must be borne in mind with respect to the introduction of a new formula concerns the question of whether provinces with stable or declining populations should lose seats in the House of Commons. The loss of seats has always been a matter of genuine concern in the Canadian system. By way of example, this is reflected in the constitutional amendment of 1915 which provided that no province would be represented in the House of Commons by a number of Members less than the number of its Senators. The legitimacy of such concerns was again recognized in 1982 when the so-called "senatorial clause" was made unamendable except with unanimous consent of the provinces. Such concerns of federal balance have led me to recommend that provinces which, on a strict numerical basis, would see their representation reduced should be allowed to keep those seats, even at the expense of absolute representation by population.
There is a third general factor which must be considered when devising a formula. It concerns provinces with growing populations. Recognition must be given to the fact that population distributions change over time. People living in provinces which enjoy population increases are entitled to expect that there will be concomitant increases in the numbers of their representatives in the House of Commons.
This reform must, if it is to be accepted, be seen to be fair. The new method of redistributing seats throughout Canada is fair because it ensures that the proportion of seats and proportion of population of each province does not significantly deviate from the present situation. This means that the relative imbalances which exist today and have long been accepted as necessary compromises on the principle of absolute representation by population will remain.
You will say that this is a typical Canadian compromise. Perhaps it is. However, in a Parliament with only one elected House, our system has come to recognize the need of finding ways of ensuring adequate regional representation in the elected body and this Bill proposes no departure from this position. It is in view of these considerations, that the formula set out in the Bill was devised.
Accordingly, it attempts to accomplish three basic objectives. First, it limits increases in membership in the House of Commons to levels as moderate as are fair and practical; Second, it ensures that no province or Territory will lose seats
October 1, 1985

in the House of Commons through redistribution. Third, it enables provinces with growing populations to get additional seats but in a way that reflects the need to maintain the House of Commons at something close to its present size. [Translation]
Mr. Speaker, this Bill not only concerns the distribution of seats throughout the country but also contains proposals aimed at improving the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act. As Hon. Members are aware, the Act regulates the procedure by which the boundaries of electoral districts are established within the provinces.

The present wording of the Act obliges commissions to ensure that all constituencies in a province have populations which are within 25 per cent of the so-called provincial quotient.
This obligation has been seen by many Members of Parliament as posing problems with respect to rural and sparsely populated areas. It forces the creation of geographically huge districts in many areas of the country.
In order to try to alleviate these problems, the Bill proposes that commissions be given some added flexibility. It suggests that, in extraordinary circumstances, they be allowed to deviate from the 25 per cent rule in order to protect an historical community of interest or to limit constituencies to a manageable geographical size, where possible.
The Bill also proposes improvements in the way in which commissions conduct their hearings. I do not believe that it should be necessary for them to publish both a map and a written description of boundaries with their newspaper advertisements, yet the current legislation requires this. If only the maps had been published for the last redistribution, a saving of approximately two-thirds of the total amount spent on advertising could have been realized. This would have amounted to approximately $1.6 million. Thus, the Bill provides that only the maps be included in the newspaper inserts. Of course, written descriptions of constituency boundaries will continue to be available, free of charge, from the Electoral Boundaries Commissions' offices.
[ Translation]
Finally, Hon. Members will now have a chance to give their views and suggestions regarding the commissions' reports. For the first time, the Bill specifically gives Members the right to submit their views to the commissions.
As well, there will be improved opportunities to debate the reports of the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Commission.
Under the old legislation, these reports were discussed on the floor of the House, whereas this Bill would see them automatically referred to a committee for consideration. Members will know of the difficulty in obtaining sufficient time to
Representation Act, 1985
consider legitimate objections to these reports on the floor of the House. Therefore, the Bill proposes to provide Members a real opportunity to have their concerns fully considered in committee with supporting documentation which can be tabled, together with an appropriate period of time which would be made available for each Member desiring to make representation in terms of any electoral district.
As I have indicated, time limits for each stage of consideration by committee of these reports which the Bill proposes ensure that redistribution takes place on a timely basis.
The House may wonder why it is important to ensure that this legislation is considered expeditiously, aside from the requirement to have the new boundaries for the ridings in place well before the next general election. I am convinced that this Bill, as part of the entire program of institutional reform, will help to modernize and make Canadians' key democratic forum an effective institution which will help to point the way to the next century. The Canadian people gave this Government a mandate for change. I believe this Bill helps to fulfil, as far as this institution is concerned, this part of our responsibility.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would like to ensure that the House is aware of the great period of renewal upon which we have embarked. Reform of this institution can only be achieved by careful attention to the reasons for its continuance and its importance in the society it serves. Reform of obscure rules and arcane practices will not necessarily make Parliament more effective. However, if we have the courage to seize this opportunity to reshape the kind of House this will be, and to raise the expectations of all Canadians for this, the most important democratic institution of our country, we will have done succeeding generations of Canadians, 1 think, a great service.
Finally, let me reiterate my belief that the proposals set out in this Bill not only represent significant improvements in the redistribution process, but also they will assist us all in the task of ensuring that the House of Commons becomes a more effective and productive institution, and that expanded, it fairly represents the population and diversity, which is Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate on Bill C-74, to amend the legislation regulating the number of seats attributed to a province in Canada after each decennial census.
First of all, I may say we understand the Government's intentions and its reasons for wanting to prevent the number of Members sitting in the House of Commons to keep on increasing at a rate that is considered too fast by some, and that, as a corollary, the Government is attempting with this measure to limit spending which is necessarily proportional to the number of Members that represent Canadians in the House of Commons.

October 1, 1985
Representation Act, 1985
Although we approve the principle or the objectives being pursued by the Government, in other words, although we agree with the reasons for the measure being proposed, we do not, unfortunately, agree with the method.
Although we believe that the Government's intentions are honourable, we think it has not chosen the right way to go about attaining its objectives. In our view, one of the consequences of the measure now before the House will be to undermine the basic principle of any redistribution of seats in Canada, in other words, the fundamental principle of proportional representation. Another consequence would be that the Bill would create an increasing imbalance between the average populations of a riding, from province to province. We also believe this might create an imbalance between the average populations of urban and rural ridings.
[DOT] (U25)
Finally, another obvious result of the procedure the Government has decided to follow is,-and I find it rather strange, since one of the Government's objectives was to limit spending connected with representation of the people of this country in Parliament,-in fact the first consequence of this Bill will be to waste about $5 million which were spent to date by the commissions of various provinces on drawing up the electoral map now before Parliament, which could be considered in a couple of hours and become effective in relatively short order. The Government ought to realize that its decisions involve at the very outset wasting $5 million.
Let me get back to what I consider to be the main weakness of this Bill. I said earlier that I thought the principle of proportional representation would be at risk. I said there would be a significant difference between the average riding population in some provinces as compared to others. In other words, if we divide the population of a province by the number of seats, the resulting quotient will vary fairly substantially from province to province. To support my statement I would refer to certain comments by witnesses who appeared before the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections, and especially to what was said by Professor Andrew Sancton, who appeared before the Committee on June 20. His testimony may be found on page 12:5 of the Committee proceedings. I am just going to quote what Professor Sancton said and comment subsequently. He said, and I quote:
When one divides the population of each province by the number of seats allocated to that province according to the new formula, one finds that the resulting provincial quotients vary to quite a considerable extent. Anyone who has made such calculations for previous redistributions would not be surprised by such a result. The smaller provinces, for one reason or another, always had smaller quotients, and to that extent they have been over-represented in the House of Commons.
What is most unusual about the current calculations is that they produce quotients for British Columbia and Alberta of 91,482 and 97,292 by my calculations, which are significantly higher than the quotients of the two largest provinces of Ontario and Quebec. I think the proper figure for Ontario is 88,919, which is corrected on some of the statements and not on others, and the one for Quebec 85,845.
We already see a sizeable quotient difference of roughly 9,000 between British Columbia and Ontario. Why does the Government tolerate from the very beginning that its proposed measure would create such significant differences, quite obviously built right into the system? As stated earlier by the President of the Privy Council and Government House Leader (Mr. Hnatyshyn), the avowed priority objective and main principle guiding the Government in drafting this Bill were to make sure that the proportional representation principle would be maintained. These figures clearly indicate that the result will be altogether different. More important still, we have to consider the long term impact of those differences. Again I quote Professor Sancton on page 12:5 of the proceedings:
Although the difference in the quotients between Ontario and Quebec themselves-
-since it is now only 3,000 in this case, since this quotient-
-is not large, there is no reason why they cannot become larger if this formula were to be applied in future decades.
There is a gap of more than 8,000-
-these figures are taken from documents provided by the Government-
-if one makes the calculations based on the census projections for 2001.
That is beginning to be quite important between two neighbouring provinces whose ridings have so far been roughly similar.
This goes to show why we do not quite agree on the way the Government seeks to achieve an objective which is highly commendable in itself.
The other matter which has me worried and which also undermines the basic principle of proportional representation is the fact that, through this Bill, the Government wants to achieve a second objective, namely make sure that none of the provinces will lose seats through the implementation of this new redistribution system. First I must say that there is nothing to underlay this principle, in the sense that, at the political level, the Government may want to protect itself against the dissatisfaction which might be expressed by the residents of a province slated to lose seats. From a logical viewpoint however, if we want to respect the principle of proportional representation, that is representation based on population, how can we argue in this House and reach the conclusion that, if the population of a province goes down or if a province realizes that its population is not increasing as rapidly as that of neighbouring provinces, we are justified to claim that such a province will not lose seats? However unpalatable this might be for the residents of that province, we must admit that it would amount to a serious breach of the proportional representation principle.
I therefore conclude that the Government is not proposing this measure to uphold the proportional representation principle but rather to cover its rear and avoid being the target of sustained flak from the disgruntled residents of a province. I
October 1, 1985

can understand that the Government would want to protect itself and limit the dissatisfaction of the population, but in my opinion, it would be better to make its pious wishes in other areas of interest, such as the bankruptcy of the banks and the tainted tuna. The Government would be better to try and prevent the dissatisfaction of the population in these areas. However, I cannot say that I agree with the fact that the Government is trying to fool around with the principle of proportional representation.
Once more, I would like to quote the comments made by some of those who appeared before the committee to object to what the Government is proposing, and I again quote from a statement by Professor Andrew Sancton as recorded on page 12:6 of the Minutes of Proceedings of the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections for Thursday, June 20, 1985. In passing, I should point out that Professor Andrew Sancton is not just anybody. He is in a good position to comment the redistribution proposals because he is professor emeritus at the Western Ontario University, where he teaches political sciences. He was also a full member of the later Ontario Electoral Boundaries Commission. He therefore knows all about this issue. Let us hear what he has to say about the provision to prevent provinces from losing seats:
My preference in all this is to fix the size of the House at about its current level and to follow the procedure outlined in the white paper but allow provinces to lose seats down to the level of the entrenched senatorial floor and to gain them to the full measure of their relative growth.
He then continued:
Sure, it will be tough for provinces to lose seats-
This is what 1 was saying earlier.
-but I suggest that the people most affected by such losses are incumbent MPs. If the real objective of this exercise is to limit the growth of the House of Commons and to maintain representation by population, then I am convinced that most people in and out of the House will understand that some provinces will have to lose seats.
In this regard, I think that the Government has tried to have it both ways. On the one hand, it tries to meet its objective of limiting the increase in the number of Members in the House of Commons, and on the other hand, it attempts at the same time to develop a system under which a province would not lose seats even if its population did not increase as rapidly as that of other provinces or even, in an extreme case, if its population were to decrease. Yet, these two principles are mutually exclusive and it is strange to see that the Government, by using an acrobatic scheme, has succeeded in combining them in one Bill.
Although we have to agree that reducing the number of Members of Parliament is a good objective, I would like to warn the Government that there are consequences one has to take into account, one of which is that Members will be called upon to service a larger population. There is nothing proposed
Representation Act, 1985
by the Government to facilitate the work of the average MP. No additional tools are offered; we have no assurances that some of the recommendations put forward in the report of the committee chaired by the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) will be put in place. On the contrary, we believe that the Member will be left with a larger population to service with no additional means. We do not see how this would benefit the people of this country.

Another aspect on which I would like to comment briefly is the issue of timing. The Minister said earlier that these measures would be implemented in time for the next general elections. This does not seem to be quite the case. The Chief Electoral Officer, Mr. Hamel, told us in committee that, if this Bill received quick passage this fall, he would be able to organize elections based on the new electoral boundaries, but only in the fall of 1988. Because of a very detailed schedule which he explained to us, he could not, for instance, organize an election in the spring of 1988 based on the new boundaries. This means that, because of the time factor and the schedule presented to us by the Government, neither the population nor any political party will know whether, in 1988, which would seem to be the most logical year to hold an election, four years after the election of the present Government, the election will be based on the present boundaries or on the new ones set in accordance with this bill.
It seems to me that it is rather important for pressure groups throughout the country to know what they can expect. It is important for political parties to know in advance whether they will plan the election based on the new boundaries or on the old ones. I maintain, Mr. Speaker, that the only one in Canada who will know on which basis the next elections will be held will be the Prime Minister because he will be the one to call the elections. So I suggest that the proposed schedule or timing for bringing this legislation before Parliament would give the party in power the upper hand, for it would be aware of both the election date and the electoral boundaries for which it must prepare itself. As to the other political parties and the various organizations which would like to exert pressure on them come election time, everybody would have to prepare for both sets of electoral boundaries, the old ones and the new ones, not knowing under which set the election would be fought.
Mr. Speaker, I think I have clearly demonstrated that this Bill has serious weaknesses. Although we can understand the Government's desire to limit the growth of the House of Commons as well as the resulting expenses, we believe that Parliament and the legislative committee to which this bill will be referred will have to consider some of the weaknesses I have just enumerated and a number of amendments will have to be made to this Bill in order to make it more acceptable to more people and political parties in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to take a long time to deal with this. While it is vitally important, I do not think it is terribly complex. I hope that we can get on with the committee deliberations at some early date. I can well appreciate the last comment that was made indicating that if this turns out to be the way the Government will ultimately go, then clearly the decision must be made quickly or else there will be some difficulties all across the country in adjusting to the changes.
Having said that, I would like to begin by expressing concerns about the direction in which the Government is going. I do not doubt for a moment that there would be general support across the country for the intention to demonstrate financial restraint. I think it is fair to say that the majority of Canadians would support that notion no matter who proposed it. Since the majority of Canadians do not pay a lot of attention to the size of the House of Commons or to the work of Members of Parliament other than when it directly affects them, I would be surprised if they were other than glad that the Government has placed such an emphasis on the need to restrain the expenditures of Parliament. I sense, however, from reading various articles and from speaking to people who are directly involved in this question, that there is little support for the way that this measure is being proposed.
I find it passing strange that a reference would be made to the guarantee that there would be no fewer Members of Parliament than there are Senators for any one region. If we wanted to bring about financial restraint, I would have thought that we might have decided to begin with the Senate. We might have decided to ask ourselves if it was appropriate to have a Senate or not. That would be a real financial restraint. Just think of what we could do with the money we would save if we did not have that group of old people from the previous administration and the current administration tripping around the other Chamber. It is interesting to talk about financial restraint and I think it is something with which everyone agrees. However, I think we could have found some place else to start looking for the restraints we need.
I would say to the Minister that we cannot achieve what I consider to be our three objectives through the structuring of this Bill. We cannot limit the size of the House while at the same time ensuring no loss of seats and guaranteeing that each citizen will, to the greatest extent possible, have an equal voice in Government. It cannot be done. Those things are inconsistent with each other. Therefore, there is no point in our trying to pretend that we can do that.
We are changing dramatically the representative system of the Government of Canada. This will not happen in the first year and not even in the second year, but with the passage of time, as we move beyond the year 2000, this measure will have a dramatic effect on the way calculations will be made and on the proportional representations of the regions of the country. Although the need to limit the number of Members of Parliament has some appeal, I would ask why we are doing it. Is it really our responsibility to say that we like things as they are and they suit us just fine? Does the congeniality of the House justify that we should keep it as it is? That is hardly a democratic principle. It may be a principle based on friendship, but if we were to carry that to the extreme, then we could argue that we only need 100 or perhaps 50 Members. Think how congenial we would be then. Look at the opportunities we would all have to take part in debates. Look at the opportunities we would have to serve on committees, assuming we could find sufficient Members to fill them.
When talking about it in this way, we begin to realize that the argument to limit the size of the House in order to preserve the congeniality of it and the opportunities for participation in debate and in committees has some appeal at first blush, but if carried to the ridiculous extreme would be totally unacceptable.
I think the argument being made by the Government is faulty. Representation by population is in fact the cornerstone of the democratic system within which we operate. Guaranteeing that the weight of one vote will be equal to the weight of another vote is a principle which we must attempt to uphold. That principle is being skewered by this particular measure. There is a democratic responsibility on the part of Hon. Members to ensure that we do not mess up the democratic system. I think that the Government is, with all the best intentions in the world, making a determination that would do just that.
The difficulty I see is that we could not, in all good conscience, argue that certain provinces ought to lose representation simply because their growth did not keep pace with others. I think it is commendable of the Government House Leader (Mr. Hnatyshyn) to say that we want to guarantee the smaller provinces representation no less than the representation they now enjoy, but in the process of doing that, I think he recognizes that it does penalize the growth areas. It could be said that it penalizes the growth areas only marginally, but that marginal penalty will grow by leaps and bounds in the course of time. Notwithstanding our best efforts, it will not be possible, come the year 2010-by which time, I hope, most of us will be gone from this place but not from this life-for those here then to redo what we have undone and to put back together what we have taken apart.
I suggest that one of the problems is in trying to find a balance between the regions in order to ensure that regions do not have a sense of alienation from the federal Government and yet, at the same time, to ensure that within those regions the representation of rural against urban areas is preserved. We should recognize that the urban areas are the growth areas and the difficulties that confront urban areas are, under normal circumstances, more complex by virtue of size and pressure than the difficulties that confront less urbanized parts of the country. In fact, it will be necessary for there to be a larger number of representatives from the growth areas, the core areas of municipalities, in order to be able to put forward adequately the many and diverse views and concerns that will

continue to arise, concerns that we probably cannot even contemplate at this point in time.
In essence, what I am trying to say is that I am not being critical of the Government for considering this measure. I think it is worth considering. I do not think, however, that it will achieve what we are trying to achieve. For example, why would we decide, when making a calculation ostensibly based on the 1971 census for the year 1991, that at some appropriate point in time we would allow for half the number of seats allowed for under the old formula? Why would we allow for only half? Why not a quarter or why not three-quarters? What is the importance of one-half? How has that been democratically determined? What does that mean in terms of representation? I do not think anyone knows. It is simply a figure drawn from nowhere. It is a number drawn from nowhere which would keep the House at a size that we could manage given the confines of the building itself, or some other determination. That is not good enough. There is room in this House for some substantial growth, if need be. I think that if the existing system, which has served us fairly well for a long period of time-

I feel that from our point of view, first, the money saving is not a lot. It depends on how you measure it. It certainly does not measure up to $1 billion for a failed bank, when you think about it. And I do not think that for the amounts of money we are talking about saving, the risks of distorting the representative system would be justified. To sum up, I am frankly not convinced that this direction is the direction we should take. I am concerned that it will unnecessarily alter the method previously used to determine the democratic representation. I am concerned that it will have an adverse effect over time on the way our provinces and Territories feel about their ability to participate in a reasonably equal way in the federal system.
I am not persuaded at this point that the savings we would derive from not having following the original formula will be sufficient to justify the change-not yet, anyway. I am prepared to listen to further argument on that. I enjoy the congeniality of the argument, but I am not sure it is a good argument for this kind of measure.
Or collegiality.

"Colleagiality" my colleague says. It is congeniality, too. With respect to the arguments about participation, I feel we can find ways to encourage further participation. We are doing it now constantly. Therefore, while I like to afford Hon. Members, as does everyone else, lots of opportunity to participate, I do not think we can do it at the expense of representation by population. I will conclude by saying to the Minister that I think the most important thing that can be done here is to get further input.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I agree.

I am persuaded from reading some of the comments which were made before the committee. Certain of those witnesses are perhaps more expert in this than 1 am- perhaps even more expert than the Minister himself, although that is hard to believe-and some of them have expressed genuine reservations, reservations which were deeply felt, that this is not the time to tinker, that it is not necessary. There is not a sufficient amount of growth in the offing that justifies this sudden readjustment.
So I say to the Minister that for the time being we certainly cannot support the proposal. We will, however, after two or three of my colleagues have commented about it, send it to committee. It will be dealt with in the committee, giving some of those who appeared before, and many others who have not yet appeared, an adequate chance to put on the record their analysis of the effects. Then we could make some further refinement, amendment or alteration to try to take into account what I think have probably been well considered views in opposition.
One point that bothers me, and I say this just in passing, is that there is always a tendency among politicians to want to safeguard their own best interests. That is true. We cannot avoid it. It is part of politics to want to protect yourself and your opportunities. We must guard agains that. We must make sure that that does not motivate us into making changes-I am not suggesting that that is the case, mind you,

October 1, 1985
Representation Act, 1985
but it is something to keep in mind. There is that sort of tendency to say that we really would like to leave things the way they are, we do not want to make any changes because, after all, it would upset the apple cart, upset the way in which we play the game. It reminds me of a comment I made when I appeared before the redistribution committee in Hamilton some time ago. They were advocating a change to my electoral boundaries and I said to them that I would welcome the change from a political point of view because it added an area which was at least 80 per cent supportice of me while taking away an area which was somewhat less than 50 per cent supportive of me. I said to them that I would be quite pleased to have it that way but I thought, quite frankly, that it was wrong. I thought that the lines they had drawn were not in keeping with the realities of the community. However, I said that if they were determined to improve my lot, if they want to give me a sinecure, almost like a seat in the Senate, perhaps there were two or three streets in the middle of my riding they could take out. That would be a damn sight better than what they were proposing. They turned it down. That is what we have to watch.
Quite frequently, our own self-interest creeps into the discussions inadvertently and, in making our arguments, we fail to see the much larger picture, and the much larger picture in this case is that we have to guarantee to the greatest extent possible that the vote of a person in one part of the country will have exactly the same weight as the vote of a person in another part of the country, that when those people vote collectively, their collective vote will have the same weight in Ottawa. I venture the opinion that although the change is marginal, and I admit it, the principle which I consider to be vital is being abrogated by the proposal before us.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate on Bill C-74, an Act to amend the Constitution Act, 1867 and the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act and to provide for certain matters in relation to the 1981 decennial census.
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this Bill is to limit the unrestrained and very costly increase in the number of electoral ridings in this country.
Historically, the Constitution Act, 1867, as amended in 1975, provided for the readjustment of representation in Commons following every decennial census. The formula for calculating the number of members would take into account the population of each province and Quebec's special situation.
The result has been a constant increase in the number of elected representatives, so that the point of saturation in the House of Commons has nearly been reached. We must remind ourselves that the House has a capacity of some 286 seats or so.
On the other hand, it was necessary to ensure that the new formula would respect the rules of equity and provincial representation, while not limiting the rate of growth of Parliamentarians and, at the same time, the operating costs of Parliament.
Mr. Speaker, I note that our colleagues in the opposition support this Bill and I am glad they do. With the method of calculating provided for under the old Bill, based on the 1981 census, there would be 310 of us here, compared with 289 with the proposed formula.
October 1, 1985

In 1991 we would have had under the former system 343 Members instead of the 291 figure resulting from the proposed formula, and in 2001, we would have 369 Members instead of the 296 under the proposed formula.
Mr. Speaker, there are concerns voiced by Members opposite who suggest the vote should be proportional. One vote recorded in this House on behalf of one constituency has to be just as representative as one vote from another constituency.
The possibility of using the Senate formula was also suggested. One could say that whenever a seat in the Commons is lost, it might perhaps be replaced with a seat in the Senate.
Under the old formula, and speaking on behalf of Quebec, we would lose one member and gain one senator this time. In 1991 we would lose four members and gain four senators, and in the year 2001 we would lose six members and gain six Senators.
Mr. Speaker, what is important in my view is to make sure that this House has elected members who adequately represent the Canadian population.
There is provision in the proposed formula to reflect regional disparities, ethnic groups or others. Reference is made to the possibility of more or less 25 percent, on the basis established at the constituency level in each Province.
Mr. Speaker, this legislation assures the provinces of the possibility of maintaining the minimum number of seats they now have; no seats will be lost. I think this was a concern that existed at any rate in my area, as in many others in Quebec; we must make sure that the Quebec representation will remain fair, with at least the existing number of seats.
If we turn to provinces where there was a larger increase .. . We know that in other provinces, for all sorts of reasons, there is some kind of a population explosion, and we now have constituencies where there may be for instance 160,000 votes, while there are constituencies in some eastern provinces which may have only 45,000 voters. The Bill will allow an increase in the number of members in that province, of course, but instead of having the number increased at such an astronomical rate as proposed, it would be increased but in a much slower way.
This will then, Mr. Speaker, result in over-all savings just as significant, and it may also allow the possibility of providing members with better tools, in order that they may better perform their work and better represent their constituents.
Mr. Speaker, under this legislation the House would keep a manageable size, and this would make it easier for all members to be heard. Often Liberal or New Democratic Members have remarked that Government members do not often have an opportunity to speak. I understand that. We are 211 here, Mr. Speaker, and I can tell you our Liberal colleagues opposite are somewhat jealous about that. But, of course, if we are to have a greater number of members speaking in this House,
Representation Act, 1985
it must keep a manageable size, with opportunities for positive interaction.
Mr. Speaker, I am especially happy that our Government has initiated this Bill, and I am convinced that Opposition Members will want to see it through in an expeditious manner, in order that we may send it without delay to the Standing Committee and enact it as soon as possible.

The cost is actually $8.9 million, for the edification of the hon. gentleman. If the Government of Canada is concerned about saving money, why is it carrying on as it is today? However, the Government said no on the basis that it wants to save money. The other example used by the Government House Leader is even more alarming to me. He said that if we increased the number of people in this Chamber we could not have meaningful debate. He said that the Government of Canada has embarked upon a new procedural change plan and that it is implementing recommendations to give Members of Parliament a greater say in what takes place in this Chamber. That is a very strange recommendation coming from the House Leader, Mr. Speaker. Of all the Governments that have been

Representation Act, 1985
elected in this country in this century, this Government should certainly not be saying that it will give Members a greater say.
The Government says that an increase in the number of seats in the Chamber may destroy representation and that an increase is not necessary because there is a new system in effect. Mr. Speaker, the fact of the matter is that Members in this Chamber will only get the freedom to speak that the Government is willing to give them. Last night we had a meeting with representatives from the Department of Employment and Immigration. A policy had been adopted by the Government of Canada on which Members of Parliament on the Government side were briefed last week and on which members of the Opposition were briefed this week. What say do we have in what was gone through? What say do Members of the House of Commons have who are, perhaps, more qualified than anyone else in the country to pass judgment on things which affect ordinary people? We get their letters and telephone calls and we know what is wrong with programs introduced in this Chamber by the Government.
Last night we were told that in order to be employed in a government program, you must have been unemployed for 24 of the previous 30 weeks. When Government members were told of that last week they knew it was wrong. They could see all kinds of pitfalls in that regulation, yet they were powerless to do anything about it. They were powerless because it was the policy of the Government of Canada, it was the ruling of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald), and that is it. Members on both sides of this Chamber know that that regulation will mean discrimination against young people and women and anyone who had the gumption to work for seven weeks in the previous seven months because they do not now qualify to go to work or even for a referral. Members on both sides know that that is wrong, but the regulation stands.
For the House Leader to say that the Government has brought in a new era in which Members of this Chamber will have input into government policy is simply not true. The Government House Leader said that we probably have too many Members in this Chamber already and that members do not have a chance to participate. The way to solve that problem is through structural change and a change in the philosophy of the Government of Canada. To profess that this has been done is simply not true. You would have to give
Members of Parliament an opportunity to originate their own terms of reference in committees of this Chamber. You would have to give Members of Parliament the understanding that their first responsibility is to represent the people of their constituencies and that they need not hesitate to criticize a Minister of their own Government.
You know what I am talking about, Mr. Speaker. In the British system Government members criticize Government Ministers. That is the custom in most of the legislatures of the British parliamentary system, or what remains of it. With the present Government attitude and the present situation in the House of Commons we are behind the other Legislatures which operate under the British system. For the House Leader to say that the Government has introduced changes and, therefore, an increase in representation is not necessary, is a pretty shallow argument.
The reason for my intervention is simply to point out-
Get to it.

The Hon. Member says "Get to it". He obviously has not been listening very carefully. The point is that the Government is robbing a seat from Newfoundland and Labrador. Why does he not ask the four Conservative Members from Newfoundland, of the seven in the House, if they are not drastically overworked? The Hon. Member is shaking his head. He does not know. The rationale given by the House Leader is that it will result in a saving of money. The Government says that it will save money, yet, as was pointed out a minute ago, it gave a billion dollar bail-out to a bank. In fact, when one adds the figures, it comes to $2.5 billion.
I could give further examples of poor management, bad decisions and waste of taxpayers' money that has taken place since the Government came to power. Yet the Government House Leader does not want to give Newfoundland and Labrador an extra seat in the House of Commons

because the Government wants to save money. There is no rationale behind that argument.
He also argued that changes that have taken place in the procedures of the House have allowed Members a greater say in Government policy. Not only has that not occurred, the opposite has taken place. Mr. Speaker, I want to bring a couple of points briefly to the attention of the House. We have come a long way from the rotten borough system that caused much of the historical concern about how members were chosen. However, I do not believe that we have alleviated the representation problems that we will face if we do not come to an understanding of what the formula should be.
Representation by population has never really worked in Canada because of our diverse country. There are areas which need representation but have very few people. Therefore, we recognize that while representation by population may have been acceptable in deciding the number of members to represent certain areas, it has not worked totally in the past. We should recognize that it will not work in the future.
In fact, it is quite possible to make a good argument against representation by population under the current structure in Canada because it is much easier for a member to represent a large metropolitan area which has a homogeneous population than to have fair representation of a much larger area which has a heterogenous population. 1 can use as an example the Prince Albert constituency as it has been proposed under the new border structure. It takes in more than half of Saskatchewan. A very small part of the population is a rural farm population. About one-third of the population is comprised of northerners who are of native ancestry and who have a very different lifestyle and interest as far as their representation is concerned. The rest of the constituency is made up of the City of Prince Albert. Not a very large city dominates a tremendously large area. Many northerners in that constituency feel it would be much fairer to have their representation based on the northern area. However, this would be more than half of

October 1, 1985
Representation Act, 1985
the Province of Saskatchewan but would consist of only about 35,000 people.
As 1 said, you can make pretty good arguments for not using representation by population. The power of a region or a province is more important in some ways than representation by the individual. For instance, Mr. Speaker, being a westerner you will recognize that over the years Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia quite often have groups claiming that we in the West do not have enough representation in the House of Commons. It does not matter what kind of representation or what Party is in power. We do not get a fair hearing because central Canada, Quebec and Ontario form such a large part of the representation in the House that in the end any decision made will be slanted toward central Canada.
In my office I have a hat that was presented to me not too long ago. There is a map on it and it says "the Republic of Western Canada". That kind of feeling in the West arises quite often. In a number of elections lately we have had the participation of the Western Canada Concept Party. Criticism is based on the fact that people do not feel the West has had real representation in Ottawa. Although we have changed Government and have more representatives in the Government, that really does not solve the problem.
The House Leader in presenting this Bill said there was a need to save money. That is a pretty spurious reason. We cannot accept that as a particularly good argument. Over a long period of time, that would not hold much water. If the population represented by a Member gets larger, services must be maintained which will cost more money anyway.
As my colleague stated earlier, if you really want to save money, let us look elsewhere. Let us look at the other place. It costs us a lot without giving the representation which we think is necessary and which should be available, in a democracy.
Let me mention a couple of historical approaches which perhaps the committee would like to look at. There are parts of Canada which, on occasion, say they would like to have representation in the House of Commons. I speak of the City of Montreal and the City of Toronto that say that maybe they should have a Government of their own. Let me give you an example from my own experience. When I first went to Nigeria, there were 12 states there. Now there are 19. When the population of a state got too large, the state was divided in half. Northern Ontario has often said it would like to be recognized as a separate province.
Never.
Oh, oh!

I know that would be an unpopular approach to that problem, but it does make some sense. If you took Montreal out of the Province of Quebec, the population of Quebec would be considerably smaller. It would, though, be a region separate from the rest of Quebec. I know this is an unpopular approach, but it is the kind of innovation we need to
look at in order to get the kind of representation which people think they should have.
What are we trying to do? Are we trying to ensure representation by population, or are we trying to ensure that every region of the country gets the kind of representation which makes it feel it is part of the country? There are many parts that do not. I know from close proximity that western Ontario feels an awfully long way from Toronto.
What about northern Ontario?
Northern Ontario does too. Even if you get as far as Sudbury, you feel a long way from Toronto.
Oh, oh!

Northern Saskatchewan felt so far from Regina that the Department of Northern Saskatchewan was formed in order to give that part of the province some representation in the Government.
Power is important to the region. Power goes with representation. If you develop a program which does not make any part of Canada feel it has representation, regardless of whether representation by population is the direction you should go- that is part of my feeling and traditionally we have gone that way-it will not work. We must recognize that representation itself is our basic concern.
Let us make sure in whatever we do to solve this problem that we give all parts of Canada the representation they think is necessary to have a voice in the Government of Canada.
Large rural areas and large northern areas need some form of representation which recognizes them as a homogeneous group. They have concerns as to how the country is governed. At the moment we would not want to support this Bill in its present form. The committee, when it looks at this Bill, can examine some of these concerns and make sure that Canadians will feel in the end they are well represented in this Parliament.

speechtext: Are there any questions or comments? If there are no questions or comments, we will resume debate. The Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria).

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate on Bill C-74. I think we should take a minute to talk about the principle of proportional representation in the House of Commons. [Translation]
I heard a while ago the Hon. Member for Portneuf (Mr. Ferland) state that he was in favour of a proportional representation system in Canada and indeed, Mr. Speaker, we have such a system but with some difference, and as you know the difference is that there is a minimum below which a province cannot go as regards its number of seats even when the population of that province is proportionally lower that
October 1, 1985

that in other areas and that minimum is the number of seats representing the province in our Senate. This means that a province which has four senators cannot have less than four members in the House of Commons.
Mr. Speaker, apart from that factor, we have to all intents and purposes a proportional representation system in our country.

We could say that in fact we have a modified system of proportional representation right now because of the guaranteed minimum number of seats represented by senators.
I should like to make a comment now, which I hope will elicit a reply later by the Government House Leader. I refer to Article 42(1) of the Constitution Acts in Canada, 1867 to 1982 which reads as follows:
An amendment to the Constitution of Canada in relation to the following matters may be made only in accordance with subsection 38(1):
(a) the principle of proportionate representation of the provinces in the House
of Commons prescribed by the Constitution of Canada;-
In its new Bill the Government is modifying the principle of proportionate representation which I have just described because it is adding a second level at which there is a guaranteed number of seats. I described the first level just a moment ago, that is, the number of seats in the Senate. There is a second level of protection, which is the present number of seats that any province has in the House of Commons. In my view it could potentially infringe upon that provision in the Constitution. It is quite clearly indicated that the only floor level shall be the number of seats in the Senate. If that is being modified, perhaps we require a constitutional amendment in order to accomplish it.
I am not saying that I am totally against what has been announced today by the Government House Leader, but I have some reservations about it. I think we should all be conscious of what we are doing. We are changing the entire system of proportional representation that we now have. From now on the existing.number of seats in the House will be the guaranteed minimum for the provinces represented by Hon. Members. That is vastly different from what we have had in the past.
Hon. Members opposite should be concerned about it. For instance, Members of Parliament representing the Province of Ontario will be representing 88,819 voters in the House of Commons, on average, after this redistribution has been completed. They should also recognize that it will cost some $5 million to effect this redistribution. We have just finished redistributing the number of seats in the House of Commons, to which all political Parties agreed at the time. If this is to be changed, I believe all Members of the House should be very conscious of these facts and of the fact that it will cost millions of taxpayers' dollars to accomplish it.
Of course, I recognize the dilemma. One redistribution called for an increase in the number of seats, bringing it to somewhere in the order of 340 seats, and therefore would have created considerable expenditures in itself. We recognize that
Representation Act, 1985
it costs approximately $300,000 or $400,000 per year for every Member of the House of Commons, that is, for support staff, office space and everything else involved. Of course, the 340 seats would have been after the next redistribution. The other redistribution we were discussing would have brought it to 310 seats, but the number we are discussing now is 288 seats. Frankly, that number is sufficient. Some Hon. Members have said in the past that if the House of Commons were represented by a number larger than that, it would become unwieldy. I tend to agree with that. In fact, at this moment I do not envy Conservative back-benchers; I would not envy anyone being a Conservative in any case. Those back-benchers have very little, if any, occasion to speak. Of course, we recognize that they do not often use whatever occasion is available to them. Nevertheless, they have very little opportunity to speak in the House because of the fact that there is a large number of Members from the same political Party. I see the Secretary of State (Mr. Bouchard) and the Hon. Member for Hochelaga-Maisonneuve (Mr. Desrosiers) sitting across the way. No doubt both of them will participate in this debate later. There are considerations on both sides of the issue about which we should be aware. I hope the parliamentary committee looking into the details of the Bill will take them into account.
I should like to turn to a local concern involving my constituency of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell.
It is well represented.

Thank you. The people in the western end of my constituency, particularly those in the Township of Cumberland, in the Regional Municipality of Ottawa-Carleton, are becoming dissatisfied with the fact that their community is divided in half. There are two municipalities for the area of Orleans, two provincial Members of Parliament, two federal ones, two municipal councils and two of everything else. This has been very divisive in the past, and the community of Orleans has requested that every attempt be made to unite that community. Particularly, the Mayor of Cumberland and the Township of Cumberland indicated that one federal Member of Parliament should represent the area. I hope the committee bears that in mind.
There is another problem involving the area, that is, rapid growth, particularly in the eastern end of Ottawa, and its effect on the constituency of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell and, for that matter, on the constituency of Ottawa-Carleton as well. According to the 1981 census, 82,706 people live in my constituency. That is what is indicated on paper, and in theory it is just about the right number in terms of representation in the House of Commons by one Member of Parliament. However, the Township of Cumberland, according to the 1981 census, had only 18,000 people. It had 25,500 by 1984 and will have 29,860 by the end of this year according to the projections of the municipal officials. By the end of next year it will have 35,159 and 46,682 by 1991. Obviously it is a rapidly

growing area. That should be taken into account in a special way when the redistribution occurs. I hope the officials doing the preparatory work will bear this in mind. Perhaps they could arrange the electoral map under the redistribution in such a way that if they use the 1981 figures, they make ridings with a smaller number of people in those areas that have experienced the recent urban growth about which we all know. The reality is that at the time of the next election we will have an electoral map with roughly the same number of constituents everywhere. I see the Hon. Member for Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid) sitting across-
He is sleeping.

He also represents a riding that has a very large number of constituents. Perhaps if such a formula, including taking into account areas of potential growth and putting a slightly lower number of people in those ridings for the purposes of redistribution, had been considered when the redistribution was made in the past, he would not have had the problem of having a constituency which is so large. For the same reason I think we are going to see the same thing happening in the constituency I represent now. We are seeing in the eastern end of Ottawa, where villages such as Orleans only had 2,000 or 3,000 people ten or fifteen years ago and are now communities of 50,000, 60,000 or 70,000 people, almost the same phenomenon that occurred in the suburbs of Toronto a number of years ago. Those responsible for preparing the electoral map should keep these rapidly growing areas in mind.
Lastly, Mr. Speaker, I believe it was the Hon. Member for Frontenac (Mr. Masse) who described the minimum representation given to provinces. He was of the view that in the past if a province lost seats in the House of Commons, it gained additional seats in the Senate, or something to that effect. That is not the case at all. The Senate level is established so that the minimum number of seats that any province has in the House of Commons is equivalent to the number of seats that that province has in the Senate. That is what the Senate minimum means. It has nothing to do with gaining additional seats in the Senate when a province loses some in the House. We have never had that situation, otherwise some of the provinces would probably be represented vastly differently in the Senate. As we know, the original allocation of Senate seats was 24 for Canada West, 24 for Canada East and 24 for the Maritimes, to be divided into 10 for New Brunswick, 10 for Nova Scotia and 4 for Prince Edward Island, had it joined Confederation in 1867, which it did not. Therefore, at Confederation the two Maritime Provinces had 12 seats in the Senate each, and they eventually lost two each when Prince Edward Island joined Confederation. That is how the present number of Senators was arrived at. It has nothing to do with losing seats in the House of Commons as such.
I bring those issues to your attention. Yes, I think that having too large a House of Commons could be unwieldy. I agree with that principle. I am frightened because we are changing the principles of proportional representation and we
are effecting that now. I hope that the parliamentary committee ensures that we do not change that principle, and I believe as well that we should ensure that we do not offend Section 42 of the Constitution, which is a possibility. I invite those experts in that field to consult the document to ensure that that will not be the case.
The only reason put forward by the Government House Leader that I do not agree with is the fact that we are doing this to save money. That somewhat frightens me as a principle, because democracy is always expensive. There are those who say that elections cost a lot of money, but compared to places that do not have elections, I still think it is a pretty good deal. Adhering to the same principle, we would not reduce the number of seats because we are going to reduce costs. That is the wrong reason and it is frightening to think that that principle might be extended to other areas.
If we want to save money, of course, we could always sell the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) new computer that he brought in this morning or the limousine of the Secretary of State (Mr. Bouchard) or we could reduce the size of the Cabinet. Of course, we could make sure that the job of the Secretary of State is well protected in the Cabinet because surely he would stay. There are many ways of saving money, but the principle of reducing the number of seats in the House allegedly to save money is somewhat frightening, I would suggest.
I invite questions, especially from the Secretary of State.

ever, the Government made its action unnecessarily divisive by failing to authorize the Commission to look for persons who committed war crimes related to the activities of powers other than Nazi Germany.

subsubtopic: SHOE MANUFACTURING-CALL FOR LONG-TERM GOVERNMENT COMMITMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the shoe manufacturing industry makes an important contribution to the socio-economic well-being of many people in the City of Kitchener. Indeed, in the Kitchener-Waterloo-Guelph-Cam-bridge area, shoe manufacturers account for some 4,500 employees who make an average annual wage of approximately $14,000, making a total yearly payroll of $63 million. These
figures do not include the hundreds more people employed in related industries, such as suppliers and sales personnel.
I urge the Government to adopt and pursue a policy of long-term commitment to the shoe manufacturing industry so that it can regain and maintain at least a 50 per cent share of the Canadian market.
Certainly competitiveness within industry is a good thing, but it must be fair. A policy commitment ensuring a 50 per cent share of the market would allow the industry to protect existing jobs, enhance its technology, improve its productivity, and create some 6,000 new jobs nation-wide. Therefore, I call upon and urge the Government to protect the shoe manufacturing industry with a policy that ensures it a 50 per cent share of the domestic Canadian market.

Mr. Speaker, once again I would like to speak to a very important subject, namely the footwear industry.
The present quotas are about to expire, at the end of November, and we are already starting to feel the disastrous consequences. I have here a document referring to the fact that Chaussures St-Georges is shutting down after employing more than 150 people.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is imperative and extremely urgent to extend the quotas for five years for 50 per cent of the market. The only argument against extension is the interests of the consumer, which I think hardly holds water, since the interests of the consumer lie in extending the quotas, and 1 would say there are several arguments in favour of doing so.
I therefore ask the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to live up to his clear and specific promise to protect the footwear industry. This is your chance to make up for many of your failed endeavours.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday three very significant events took place. First the Northland Bank collapsed. Second, the Government stifled debate on Bill C-70, the first step in its plan to reduce the deficit on the backs of Canadian families. Third, the latest Statistics Canada figures showed that the real incomes of families are down and real poverty is up.

Families are the foundation of Canadian society. They are the institutions entrusted with the care and nurturing of our next generation, yet one in every five Canadian children now lives in poverty. Many are lining up at food banks while Governments stand idly by doing nothing.
Cutting family benefits and increasing family taxes will not help. Instead of closing down the Northland Bank, the Government should be closing down food banks. Instead of giving $1 billion to the banks, it should increase family benefits. The Government must begin to show some commitment and support to families by stopping the cut-backs in family benefits and reindexing the family allowance. Mr. Speaker, last week the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) announced that a draft tripartite agreement on beef and pork price stabilization programs had been sent to the provinces and producer associations, for comment and, we hope, approval.

He thereby deprived Quebec farm producers of their right to be represented by the Minister of Agriculture of their province within the framework of a national consultation process that is important to the future of a healthy agricultural industry in Canada.

In the light of the results of such a study, adjustments will be necessary to ensure that producers in one province do not get more government assistance than producers in other provinces.

subsubtopic: FEED FREIGHT ASSISTANCE PROGRAM-IMPORTANCE TO EASTERN LIVESTOCK INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in 1941 the Feed Freight Assistance Program was introduced. It provided for the payment of 90 per cent of the costs of transporting grain from the Lakehead to eastern Canada. Between 1967 and 1976 the level of feed freight assistance slipped to 59.3 per cent of transportation costs, and the area to be equalized was arbitrarily moved east to Montreal.
Based on the promise of feed cost equalization, a vibrant and significant livestock industry has been built. The food and agricultural sector is the most important component in the maritime economy accounting for one-third of our total jobs. The livestock industry and its supplemental farm supply and processing industries contribute more than $1 billion a year to our maritime economy. Unfortunately, this growth has not been accompanied by research, technical development, or interest in grain production in the maritime provinces.
In 1982 the Maritime Farmers Council made a proposal to the Government of Canada which is designed to achieve greater independence for the maritime agricultural industry. It calls for the maintenance of the livestock industry and the development of feed self-sufficiency in the maritimes.
We look forward to achieving greater independence. The Feed Freight Assistance Program is an important part of the proposal to achieve that result. We look forward to an early announcement confirming the continuation of this program, an important instrument of regional development.

Mr. Speaker, I have some concerns about the Bill and, like others in my Party, this morning I would like to see this Bill referred to committee so we can do some real questioning. I want to spend a few minutes this afternoon just talking about the whole process of redistribution in this country and the whole electoral system because I think the whole system probably needs a real overhaul. First, I believe very strongly that we must have representation by population. My colleagues, such as the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) who have big ridings, have a point when they say that there must be representation by population in a democratic system. However, in any democratic system, we also need

October 1, 1985
