representation by region or geography. Those are the two conflicting principles that we have not quite resolved.
The American system has resolved this conflict. In the American Senate, every state, regardless of its size, has two Senators. Whether it is Rhode Island or California, North Dakota or New York, they all have two Senators, so there is representation by region in the Senate of the United States. A small state, through the electoral process, is able to elect Senators to the American Senate and that state then has as much clout as a larger state. We do not have a system like that in this country.
First, in Canada we have an appointed Senate. I think that is a tremendous slight on our democratic image. It is a throwback to a couple of hundred years ago. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) can appoint any of his pals as Senators until the age of 75. This is supposed to be a democratic country. Most Canadians would like to see the Senate as it exists now abolished. If we do keep a second Chamber, we should have it as an elected body so that the people can vote for those who sit in the other place.
I would like to suggest this afternoon that we send this matter to the committee and discuss issues other than the addition of six seats, something that merely delays the ultimate decision and is like putting a band-aid on a wooden leg. It does not resolve anything. Let us have a really good discussion in committee about the kind of representation we wish to have. There are a great many new Members of all Parties in the House of Commons. I think now is a good time to make a break with the past.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Regina West, sat on a special committee of this House on redistribution in 1969-70. Back in those days, we kept trying to solve the problem of representation by population and representation by region by adding Member after Member. This place is growing like Topsy. We have gone from 265 Members to 284 Members. The next proposition is to have 290 Members. Soon we will have over 300 Members. I suggest that that does not solve the problem. It simply makes this place more bureaucratic, expensive and frustrating.
Where are you going to put them all?

My friend asks where we would put them all. At that time it was suggested that we take out the back doors, knock down the end wall and add another 50 or 60 seats. Another suggestion was to take down the curtains and put in two extra rows, or to do like the British House in which there is not a seat for each individual Member. Benji and I could use the same seat. One day I would use it, and the next day he would use it.
Oh, no.
I do not think that that is the way we want to go. That is certainly not the way I want to go.
I'll take Benjamin.

That would not help the small provinces. Saskatchewan now has 14 Members in a House with approximately 280 seats. It would not make any difference if we had 20 Members in a House with approximately 400 seats. We would have no more clout. We would simply spend a lot more money and make the system more bureaucratic. We would slow down the entire process and increase the frustration of Members.
I would argue that we need to look at the entire system. We should try to come up with a system that recognizes representation by population on the one hand and representation by region or geography on the other. We may, for example, decide that we ought to have rep by pop in this Chamber and have rep by region in another elected chamber, a chamber with equal representation from all provinces. This would reflect the wishes of people at the provincial level. Each province would have a certain number of Senators. That way, we could have a melding of rep by pop with rep by region or geography. I think it is very important that we do that.
The present system will become very distorted, bulky and cumbersome. The electoral boundaries map proposed by the former Parliament contains some very strange looking ridings. In Saskatchewan, for example, there are now two urban seats in Regina and two urban seats in the City of Saskatoon, two of which are a little bit rural. Under the new proposition, there will be three seats in the City of Saskatoon and three in the City of Regina, and a few of those seats in each case will be almost half urban and half rural. The proposed new riding of Regina East, for example, will be about 50 per cent urban and 50 per cent rural. Those who live in rural areas have nothing in common with people who live in the cities. We get these strange boundaries because of the kind of system we have.
As well, there are all kinds of unique situations in this country. Labrador, for example, is an entity by itself and is different. Perhaps we should have a seat for Labrador. I know my colleagues from northern Ontario will be speaking later on about the uniqueness of their region. Their concern is that if we go strictly for rep by pop, there will be a loss of seats in the northern part of the Province of Ontario. There is also the unique factor of Quebec and Francophone Canada and the need for a protection of representation for Francophone Canadians. The same thing is true, of course, of native Canadians.
My main purpose in rising today is to suggest to my colleagues that we not do this on a piecemeal basis by adding two seats to Ontario, two seats to British Columbia and two seats to Alberta. Rather, we should refer this entire matter to the committee so that it can look at the whole process of representation and try to meld together rep by pop and rep by geography.
Right now there is discontent in various parts of the country. People feel alienated and left out of the system. There have been western separatist movements and unrest in Quebec. There has been alienation felt by native people and those in northern Ontario. I think we must look at the system in terms of trying to protect those differences.

Another point I would like to make is that there is a difference between rural and urban ridings. Urban Canada, and particularly the suburban ridings, can be a homogeneous community composed of people with very similar problems. Many Hon. Members say that that is not so because every individual has a different problem. However, in a rural riding like mine, there are 60 communities, eight Indian reserves and tens of thousands of square kilometres. There are radical cultural differences between one end of the riding and the other. It makes it rather unfair for those who represent rural ridings. If there were a melding of rep by geography and rep by pop, those differences would not be as important. Members with huge, sprawling rural ridings would be allowed extra staff or an extra allowance or whatever it would take to represent the riding adequately. That is not done today except in the case of seats in the Far North.
I suppose one could go on to mention a number of other things that are very important in terms of representation but I would like to stop here and make an appeal. We live in a great country with much diversity between regions and provinces. Rather than adding a few seats every now and then, perhaps we ought to postpone this entire process until the 1991 census, at which time we could make a general proposition that will change the entire system to make it more reflective of what Canadians really want. The Americans and the Swiss have accomplished this. We may not necessarily want to take those routes. Perhaps we would like to have one chamber with the melding of the two systems right here. Perhaps we could have a constitutional floor for the smaller provinces so that in Saskatchewan, for example, no matter what the population would be, there would still be 14 Members. Members from Toronto and Montreal might have twice as many electors as we have. Perhaps that is the way we will go. However, by not analysing and studying the whole thing, all we are doing is postponing making a decision and we could stumble right back into the old decision, which was to keep adding 30, 40 or 50 members after every census. I believe that is going the wrong way and making it a much more costly, complicated, bureaucratic and frustrating chamber in which to represent the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, in addressing the questions posed by Bill C-74, I would like to, first, go back a little in the history of redistribution and, indeed, on the idea of proportional representation. Obviously the idea of proportional representation within a democratic system has been around for a number of centuries. However, it is equally evident that the population shifts and changes in balance of population which necessitated redistribution were not evident in the then very few democratic societies until the time of the industrial revolution.
I believe that while we can fairly state that both the American and French revolutions were founded in the initial structuring of their democratic chambers on proportional representation, the first serious effort at redistribution took place in the United Kingdom during the reform period in the 1840s, I believe-
Eighteen thirty-two.

My colleague tells me it was 1832, and I thank him for the correction. The pre-reformed Parliament of the United Kingdom was characterized by vast differences in representation, not only in terms of quality, obviously, but also

October 1, 1985
Representation Act, 1985
in terms of the area and the population represented by an individual Member of Parliament. It was said in those days that there were some Members of Parliament who literally had no constituents. The Borough of Higham Ferrers was frequently mentioned as being almost entirely depopulated yet still having two Members of Parliament to represent it. In those times they had this archaic mechanism, which one would hope, of course, never to see perpetuated in this day and age, of a two-Member constituency. Therefore, Higham Ferrers, with very few people, was electing two Members to the House of Commons as were, indeed, many heavily populated boroughs and parts of the City of London.
There were also, interestingly enough, seats established for the Universities of Oxford and Cambridge, another precedent which perhaps we would not want to see repeated in this day and age. The debate in those times was the degreee to which Members should represent equal population units within the country, equal numbers of people. Of course, there were those at that time who spoke out against redistribution on the grounds that it was best to play it safe and stick with what tradition and history had hallowed and sanctioned, that there was no advantage to be gained in having Members of Parliament actually represent people, let alone the same number of people.
Moving through history, we can see the sad tale of the redrawing of constituencies to suit the narrow political interests of a single Party, always, of course, the Party in power. It was said that a type of press conference, a public meeting was held in one of the southern states of what is now the United States-I forget which one it was-and someone pointed to the map and said to Governor Gerry, "But this. Sir, looks like salamander". He replied, "No, sir, that is a gerrymander". So the term "gerrymandering" passed into the language.
I am glad to see that we are not today confronted by a situation of gerrymandering or Rotten boroughs, however much some of us may feel that some boundary changes do not reflect community reality or the sense of the constituency which had grown up in the area. Rather, we are faced with the overhauling-and, I dare say, it is not exactly overhauling but more tinkering-of a typical Canadian practice in which inequities have been reduced but then left unattended with the obvious result that inequities of a new and different nature creep in and are then themselves institutionalized and hallowed by tradition.
I believe there are a number of examples in the present representations in Canada which I would like to speak about. Perhaps, first, I should say that I believe that what we are engaged in today, and what I hope the committee will take very seriously, is a task of great gravity and significance and one which should be accorded due attention, for it is nothing more or less than the maintenance function in our democratic system. It is said that one can have the greatest architect in the world, the most beautiful and most technically elegant design, but none of it is any good unless there is a plumber around to fix the pipes. That is a paradigm of which we should be very cognizant. In a sense we are in the position of the plumber who
has to fix a little more than the pipes. It is rather more significant and we should devote our attention to that maintenance task with a full appreciation of the gravity it entails.
What is it, Mr. Speaker, that really governs the divisions of our constituencies as they exist today? I am afraid to say it appears that the number one determinant of those constituency demarcations is that of history; where the population was in the past, sometimes 100 years ago. I am also afraid to say that the Canadian tradition of gradualism has led to some areas of the country being grossly under-represented. 1 am afraid to say, also, that in the drawing of constituency boundaries great attention has been paid to lines of latitude and longitude and very little to lines of communciation, be they physical or cultural. Some attention has indeed been paid to geography but I suggest that the weight given to geography is such, and done in such an unsystematic fashion, that it does not fundamentally serve to recognize the effect of geography on the nature and quality of the representation that Members of Parliament are able to give their constituents.
There are several examples which I would like to draw out and, lest I be accused of favouritism or merely priming the parish pump in my own constituency, I would start with the City of Scarborough and its federal ridings. I acknowledge that the people in that burgeoning suburban area of Metropolitan Toronto are indeed under-represented when we see the number of electors who elect a single representative in that area. In revising our system of representation we should be taking into account the very real and legitimate concern of citizens of places like Scarborough and adjust boundaries and allocations of representation accordingly. We should also look at the example of the Northwest Territories where we have enormous geographic areas, where either of two constituencies is capable of encompassing the same geographical area as perhaps 150 of the smaller constituencies. The population is culturally and ethnically very different from the majority of Canadians in the provinces. It is not my purpose to say that, because each of the constituencies in the Northwest Territories encompasses far fewer people than the average constituency in the provinces, we should be reducing the number of seats in that area. I think the problems of geography and communications, and the differences in culture, must be adequately recognizes by our system. Let us bear in mind, after all, that the number involved are not of an excessive order of magnitude in my interpretation, being something in the order of three or four to one. I would also like to take the example of Prince Edward Island. That province is a place, and the Islanders a people, which I cannot praise highly enough. I spent my first Canadian holiday ever in Prince Edward Island and enjoyed it greatly. Yet we must question the provisions which fix the representation of that province to a number of people per constituency which is almost exactly the same as the number in the Northwest Territories.
Redistribution must not be a process which swims against trends. It must be a process which follows trends but with a reasoned gait, a measure of caution, and a step which does not
October 1, 1985

either overly weight the past or overly discount the visible trends going into the future.
I would like to also turn to my own constituency and instance the problems of an area which is slightly larger than Germany, that is both the Federal and the Democratic republics put together, and which has 110 communities spread out over most of the area, not all concentrated in one single part.
I, or indeed anyone else who represented that constituency, would be physically incapable of providing the sort of representation that every Canadian ought to enjoy and which should be extended to a number of communities, more than 20, which have no road access. I feel in a sense a prisoner of the present system's not taking into account the geography of this country, not taking into account the difficulties of transportation and communication, and above all, in that context, not taking into account the very special and unique situation of the first peoples of this country with a cultural tradition which is very much under threat-not under deliberate attack but nevertheless under threat-by the majority trends in our society. I believe that just as is done in the Northwest Territories, the boundaries of constituencies ought very much to take account of the differences between people. Where there are obvious identifiable ethnic groups, that should be something that is taken into account in the drawing of constituencies. Unfortunately, that is not the case. The Nishnawbe-Aski Nation, as the Cree and Ojibway people of northern Ontario in my constituency are known, are sliced by those lines of longitude up and down the map. There is no relation to geography, no relation to tradition, culture or the traditional or present day economies of the area. They are divided between four constituencies and thus is their collective interest and political voice muted in the conduct of the affairs of this nation. I am afraid to say that is not the only instance where tradition and culture and geography have been ignored in the formulation of constituency boundaries. In reference to that 1 would like to congratulate my friend, the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster), on the introduction of his Bill which proposed to fix the representation of northern Ontario at the number of ridings it has today rather than lose ridings in an area which is so vast and so hard to represent because of an internal redistribution process within the Province of Ontario.
It is a phenomenon of the democratic process that only when a certain mass of support or pressure gets behind an issue is there really a serious examination of that issue. I would suggest that in examining the issue of redistribution we should also examine some connected and related issues. It has been suggested that there would be a considerable financial saving by limiting the expansion of this House. I, for one, am not one to advocate an extension of the House except at the most modest pace because I do not believe that a new varnish of additional layers of Members at every general election will obscure some of the flaws presently inherent in the system. I would rather see us do with approximately the number of Members we have today. However, we also have other entrenched formulas which would appear to compel the increase in the House. One of these, of course, is the relation
Representation Act, 1985
postulated between the number of seats in this House on a province-by-province basis, and the number of seats in the Senate. I am sure you, Mr. Speaker, would not be surprised to hear me say that the best way to get out of that particular dilemma would be to abolish the Senate. I have observed in this House, and in many other places, that that is not a democratic institution but an anti-democratic institution functioning at the heart of an otherwise democratic society. My belief is that if the saving of money is an objective, the saving by abolishing the Senate would be twenty times what the addition of six seats to this House would cost. Therefore, that question should also be brought before the committee when this Bill is referred to it.
I would like to go on at some length about the principles which underlie representation by population and I can see, Sir, that you are only too willing to hear me, even if others might not be. However, I will content myself with these final observations. When this Bill comes to committee there is a far larger number of factors which need to be considered than have been postulated by the Government side. The process of consideration should be undertaken in a far more serious and effective fashion than seems to be predicated.

There being no questions or comments, I recognize the Hon. Member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McCrossan) on debate.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today because I think this issue is one of very serious concern to my constituents. My riding of York-Scarborough is so well known that three of the last four speakers have referred to it as being the most populous riding in the country. It has been the most populous riding in the country for approximately 30 years even though we have had roughly three redistributions. It would remain the most populous riding in the country under the redistribution which was proposed in the last Parliament. This points out certain problems which I believe are addressed in this Bill in a positive way. I would like to indicate my support for the Bill because I think that, for the first time, we see a hint of something which will make the redistribution process fair for those people who live in the rapidly expanding suburbs of our country, particularly Metro Toronto.
The Bill as proposed does two things which I support. First, it slows down the rate of growth of the House which should have a considerable effect in savings. At the same time it offers protection to certain regions of the country in two different forms. There is protection for provinces such as Prince Edward Island, for the northern areas of the country, and for the Northwest Territories under Clause 2 of the Bill which says that the number of representatives of any area shall not decline. Clause 6 of the Bill states that special consideration shall be taken of northern and very large, sparsely populated regions in drawing up the electoral boundaries. For the first time, in Clause 6 there is also a provision that in

October 1, 1985
Representation Act, 1985
drawing the boundaries the commissioners should try to take steps to ensure that each electoral district in the province remains more or less within the 25 per cent average of the province. It is that particular part of the Bill which I feel is the most important part for the rapidly expanding areas, and one which I endorse whole-heartedly.
As an example, when my riding was redistributed in 1978 it was, as I mentioned, the largest riding in the country. At that time there were roughly 155,000 voters and a population of nearly 300,000. That is about 12 times the size of the smallest riding. That riding was divided into the ridings of Don Valley East, Scarborough Centre and York-Scarborough. From the 1979 summer election to the 1980 winter election, a brief period of nine months, the remaining part of York-Scarbor-ough increased by 9,000 voters, a thousands voters a month. The riding of York-Scarborough now has almost 50,000 more voters than it had when it was first created.
The direction to the commissioners to take into account the trends in growth in various areas of Canada to try to ensure that each riding remains within the limit for the ten-year period is very important. If such a limit had existed at the last redistribution, they would not have lumped all of the remaining farmland in Metropolitan Toronto into my riding. They could not have conceivably done it. They could not have set up the ridings of Brampton-Georgetown, York North, or Mississauga North, the other three ridings in the country which have over 100,000 voters. The average riding has close to 40,000 voters. The ridings which I just mentioned were all growing very rapidly. That was known at the time redistribution came into effect in 1978, yet there was no direction whatsoever to the commissioners to take account of anything other than the numbers of the 1971 census or indeed, this time, the numbers of the 1981 census. It is because that particular provision gives direction to the commissioners that I feel this Bill deserves the support of the House. It will rectify a very serious inequity which has existed in my region of the country for many, many years.

speechtext: Are there questions or comments on the Hon. Member's speech? There being no questions, I recognize the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly).

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak on Bill C-74 which amends our Constitution with regard to the redistribution formula. I am very concerned, both as a Canadian and as a British Columbian, about the effects of this Bill. As a Canadian I see Bill C-74 as one more step away from the principle of representation by population. As a British Columbian I am very concerned that the historical imbalance in our representation in the House of Commons will not only continue, but will be made worse.
Bill C-74 victimizes the provinces of British Columbia and Alberta and, to a lesser extent, the Province of Ontario. The Province of Ontario is victimized to a lesser extent because at the present, on the basis of the 1981 census, it takes a smaller
population in Ontario to elect a Member to the House of Commons than it does in British Columbia or Alberta. This will have a lesser effect on the Province of Ontario because our national political life is already dominated by the Province of Ontario which holds 95 seats and the Province of Quebec which holds 75 seats. The two western provinces, which have had population growth in the last few decades, have not had that kind of clout in the House of Commons. The introduction of this Bill, which restricts the rate at whch they will be able to attain proper representation, directly penalizes the voters of those two provinces.
Redistribution is always a rough tool with which to try to provide some equity of representation in a country such as Canada which has constant population shifts. The population of one area grows while that of another declines or remains static. The machinery for redistribution has always been rather cumbersome and redistribution has, therefore, always been seven or eight years behind the population growth and the census which reports on it. For example, the 1971 census showed very clearly that there should be increased representation for the Province of British Columbia but that was not taken into account in the House of Commons in the 1972 or 1974 elections. It was not until 1979, eight years after the census, that British Columbia had the increase in the number of Members of Parliament that the 1971 census indicated we were entitled to have. What was only a lag in previous provisions for redistribution will now become a permanent disability. Provinces like British Columbia are being made victims of previous agreements made to be generous to some of the smaller provinces.
Bill C-74 enshrines those provisions in our Constitution. It enshrines the doctrine that no province will, ever have a decrease in the number of MPs, no matter what population shift might take place. This is a very generous provision that is made to some of the provinces that suffer from population decreases or have a fairly stable population growth. However, it works directly against the interests of provinces like British Columbia and Alberta which have suffered historic discrimination in the whole question of representation in the House of Commons.
When the doctrine that no province should ever suffer a decrease in its representation in the House of Commons takes precedence over the principle that there should be some equity in the representation that different parts of the country have in the House of Commons, then we have moved very far from the basic principles of democracy. The reason we have moved from that principle is that the Government has decided that it does not want a dramatic increase in the number of seats for Members of Parliament. It says that it will be too expensive. Other Members from our Party have pointed out that if the Government is really concerned about the expense of operating the Parliament of Canada, there should be some fundamental reform. The Hon. House Leader himself knows that what needs to be done is to abolish the Senate.
October 1, 1985

The previous redistribution formula tried to protect the historical number of MPs from some of the smaller provinces and to provide increased representation for provinces that had population growth. However, it was only able to do that by increasing the number of Members of Parliament as a whole. Now, the Government says that we cannot increase the number of Members of Parliament as a whole and, as a result, the entire move toward greater equality in terms of representation suffers.
In any conflict between these two doctrines-the doctrine of equality of representation and the doctrine that no province should ever lose the number of seats that it already has in the House of Commons-I believe that the doctrine of equality of representation should be paramount. However, Bill C-74 reverses that and the doctrine of equality of representation has lost out to the doctrine that no province should ever lose the number of MPs it presently has. During his speech, the Government House Leader said that it represented a typical Canadian compromise. Perhaps it is a typical Canadian compromise but democracy will still be the loser from this compromise. The long-term cumulative effects will hurt and further distort the social, economic and political union of Canada.
I do not think it can be said that somehow the population size is balanced by the geographic size of the different ridings because that is simply not the case. Let me present a dramatic example from the Province of British Columbia-the riding of Skeena. It is the largest riding in British Columbia in terms of geography and the tenth largest riding in Canada. It has 253,472 square kilometres, which is almost twice the combined size of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. There are 64 different communities in the riding of Skeena, all of which have diverse problems. Apart from major centres such as Prince Rupert, Terrace, Kitimat and Smithers, the riding of Skeena has a number of Indian villages, some of which are extremely isolated. The riding consists of isolated light houses, logging camps, mining towns and isolated ranches.
Many of these areas can only be reached by boat or charter plane. Some of these communities must be reached by the Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) travelling into the Yukon and then back down into British Columbia. Obviously, it is difficult to serve this riding which covers an area which is almost twice the size of Provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island combined.
In terms of population, Skeena is the second smallest riding in British Columbia with 75,509 people, 40,000 of whom are voters. Skeena, with its huge and difficult geographical area, had a larger population than 6 of 11 seats in Nova Scotia; 7 of 10 seats in New Brunswick; a larger population than all 4 seats in Prince Edward Island, 9 out of 14 seats in Manitoba; 11 out of 14 seats in Saskatchewan and 24 of 75 seats in Quebec. Skeena has a larger population than six urban Montreal ridings and a larger population than four Toronto ridings. This illustrates the kind of imbalance which exists in the present system of redistribution.
Representation Act, 1985
Comox-Powell River is another British Columbia riding with abundant geography. Many of the communities must be reached by boat and plane. It comprises 84,664 square kilometres which makes it larger than either Nova Scotia or New Brunswick. Yet Comox-Powell River, in its 1981 population, had 121,000 people. It is much larger than the Canadian average.
Therefore, we must ask how people in ridings like this, that are difficult to reach in the First place and difficult to travel within, can be expected to have some equality of service and access compared with downtown Montreal or Toronto ridings, some of which have populations that are less than two-thirds of the population of the riding of Comox-Powell River.
I want to stress that this is not a partisan issue. The riding of Cariboo-Chilcotin, held by a very respected Conservative Member of the House, has 111,474 square kilometres and a population of 85,000. The ridings of Kootenay East-Revel-stoke, Prince George-Bulkley Valley and Prince George-Peace River all are huge ridings that have populations of over 80,000. Again, I compare those ridings comprising huge areas with some of the ridings that have much smaller areas and populations in other provinces of Canada.
There is a different problem with respect to the suburbs. The riding of Surrey-White Rock-North Delta has the largest population in British Columbia, with 137,642 according to the 1981 census. Four other suburban ridings-Mission-Port Moody, North Vancouver-Burnaby, Richmond-South Delta and Fraser Valley West have populations of over 120,000.
There is a similar situation in Alberta where there are 21 ridings with an average population of over 100,000. This is not fair when one compares it with the situation inother provinces. Calgary East has a population of 155,450, according to the 1981 census. Calgary South has a population of 140,677; Edmonton North has a population of 127,931 and Pembina has a population of 138,712. I expect to hear from some of the Alberta Conservatives speaking out on this issue. I think it is of great concern to them as I know it is to you, Mr. Speaker.
I do not believe we can deal with this kind of a problem in a patchwork fasion. We need to make a decision on principle. I suggest if Members on all sides of the House sit down and think about the principles involved, they will agree that the first one should be fairness in representation in accordance with shifts in population. Once wy accept this first principle, we can, if we want, accept a secondary principle, namely, that within reasonable limits no province should suffer a decrease in the number of Members of Parliament who represent it.
In accepting that secondary principle, we must realize we need to increase the total number of Members of Parliament, otherwise we will end up protecting a secondary principle at the expense of a first principle. I find this unacceptable. Unfortunately that is what Bill C-74 does and I find Bill C-74 unacceptable. I hope the Government will take a hard look at this whole question of principles when we look at this Bill in committee.

October 1, 1985
Representation Act, 1985

Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the Hon. Member on his speech and the feeling he described about some of these very large constituencies. It is very difficult for any Members to serve constituents of such large ridings.
One of the principles we have at the present time in Section 42 of the Constitution of Canada talks about representation by population. This is a modified principle of representation by population that we have used all along. When I say modified, it refers to the base established by the number of Senate seats in any province. Apart from that, we have generally gone with representation by population. The more we see the urbanization of our country, the more we seem to be having problems in that regard. The rural ridings are getting bigger and bigger. The Hon. Member has just described how his constituency is already very large. How does he see reconciling on the one hand representation by population as a system in order to apportion the representation of this House while on the other hand trying to give some kind of a balance whereby we will not end up 20 years down the road with half a dozen members representing two-thirds of the physical land mass? Maybe we will not be quite that far, but we are certainly going in that direction.
In my own case, although my riding is much smaller, at one time in the past there was a Member for Glengarry, a Member for Prescott and a Member for Russell. As you know, Mr. Speaker, I represent all of Prescott, all of Russell, three-quarters of Glengarry and part of Ottawa-Carleton. That shows the shift of population and what is happening. I invite the Hon. Member to comment on that.

Mr. Speaker, the question points to one of the basic problems that any redistribution formula that does justice to Canada will have to look at if we are to depart from the basic formula of representation by population-we have moved a long way from that already-that there should be some basis on which there would be a recognition of geographic area.
As I pointed out in my speech, there is no recognition of that at present. We have a situation where a riding like Skeena, the tenth largest riding in Canada, has a population larger than the population in many ridings, including many urban ridings.
We have the situation of Comox-Powell River which has a very large and difficult area to serve because of the nature of coastal British Columbia. It has a population of over 120,000. In British Columbia, we suffer from having very large areas and from having very large populations. We are very proud of the kind of geography we have but it makes it very difficult to serve. All we are asking for is a little equity. We are not getting that in Bill C-74.

I am trying to identify in my own mind how we would establish such a system Mr. Speaker. At the present time we have one base which is a representation by populaton. We add a further ingredient, which is the number of Senate seats in one province. Today with this new Bill we have a third form, which is the existing number of seats within a province.
Am I hearing a suggesiton that we should also have another mechanism which recognizes land mass as a form of a base to be incorporated in all of this? I recognize that whoever will be doing the redistribution will have a very complicated formula by the time we get to the end. Nobody said it would be easy. Am I correct that, according to the Member, we should have another form of base; beyond a certain number of square kilometres or square miles that that would guarantee representation as well?
Mr. Speaker, I would appreciate it if the Hon. Member would not try to put words in my mouth.
I was not doing that.

I was not making that suggestion as part of my basic presentation. I was pointing to the inequity in the present situation, the fact that provinces like British Columbia and Alberta suffer from an historic gap. I said I would be open to the development of some kind of a formula that would take account of geography as well as population. 1 think that whole question has to be looked at very carefully before we opt for it.
The Hon. Member brought forward the very real problem that as we have growth in urban areas resulting in larger and larger populations, we will have a corresponding decrease in the percentage of the population who live in more isolated areas. There has to be some way of looking at that, and I suggested perhaps there could be a formula.
1 am not prepared at this time to suggest what that formula should be or what it should contain. That is something for the committee look at.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my riding takes in the Humber Valley, a large land mass, a river and a mountain chain which go through the central part of western Newfoundland. That explains Humber. Port-au-Port is a large peninsula unto itself, 200 miles south. St. Barbe refers to the St. Barbe northern peninsula of Newfoundland. It runs about 200 miles north from the Humber Valley. In total, it consists of a land mass of about 500 miles of coastline with some 90,000 souls. That is an accurate description of my riding.
I should like to take this opportunity to support what was said by the previous speaker. In the system of representation which now exists in the Parliament of Canada, there is no recognition or substantial distinction between large rural ridings and urban centres. In my judgment that distinction is not made either in respect of determining electoral boundaries nor in respect of determining Members' services.
We are all Members of Parliament. We all take our responsibilities seriously. We rise in our places to speak and to put forward our views and the views of our constituents. We all have offices. We were all elected by vote. However, that is where the similarity between an urban and rural Member stops. Our system is designed, with slight exception, to provide nearly identical services and resources to all Hon. Members. That system does not recognize the incredible and dramatic difference in the work of and the requirements on a rural Member of Parliament and those of an urban Member of Parliament. It is a serious flaw which leads to unequal service being offered to constituents, depending upon whether they live in downtown Toronto or in Cook's Harbour, on the tip of the great northern peninsula in Newfoundland. That is unfortunate, but it is something with which we can deal with in the Standing Committee on Management and Members' Services.
Bill C-74 proposes to limit or to place, theoretically, some kind of cap on unending growth or increase in the number of members sitting in the House. I can understand that, and I have some sympathy for the fact that there is a limit on how many Members of Parliament can sit in this Chamber, or in any Chamber for that matter, and provide good Government. As the previous speaker suggested, the Bill is flawed in that it contains no recognition of the huge geographic land masses regardless of population which some Hon. Members represent.
Representation Act, 1985
In the previous Bill there was to be an increase in the number of members because the principle of representation by population was acknowledged. However, even that old Bill made no recognition of geographic land mass.
I should like to refer to the situation facing those of us in the Province of Newfoundland and Labrador. The land mass of Labrador exceeds the size of the Island of Newfoundland, the Province of Prince Edward Island, the Province of Nova Scotia and the Province of New Brunswick. This area called "Labrador" does not have its own Member of Parliament. The communities of Labrador are not accessible, except by air, for six months of the year. That land mass and its various communities are not accessible by road any time of the year. At least in the summertime there is air and water transportation. People literally live thousands of miles apart in communities separated by thousands of miles of open tundra and northern terrain. There is no means of contact except by air. The people in this land mass do not even have a single Member of Parliament to represent their interests.
When one considers that to be available in a Labrador community, a Member of Parliament has to fly from Ottawa to Montreal, on to Newfoundland and then to Goose Bay, to pick up a chartered boat to sail up to Nain, one begins to understand the demands on a Member of Parliament serving not only Labrador but a good chunk of the Province of Newfoundland. One also begins to appreciate that the Parliament of Canada has not done justice either to the Member or Parliament or to the people of Newfoundland and Labrador in not recognizing their need for a separate Member of Parliament. The current Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey) has been eloquent and persistent, in the interests of the people of Labrador, in suggesting, as the Member of Parliament who currently represents all of Labrador and a good chunk of Newfoundland, that his riding needs to be split, that Labrador needs its own Member of Parliament. Yet, we see absolutely no recognition in Bill C-74 of that huge geographic land mass.
I chuckle when I think about urban ridings. God bless their Members of Parliament; they work hard and their demands are certainly as much as mine. However, I think they are able to do more with their time than I am. I chuckle when I hear them talk about a tough weekend. When I want to return to my riding to meet with the fishermen of Port au Choix who have had a disastrous year, for example, I leave Ottawa at 7.15 in the morning. I leave Montreal at 10.05 and I arrive at Stephenville at 1.30; I jump in a car and I arrive at Port au Choix five hours later, at 6.30, at which point I start my meeting, a meeting for which departed 11 hours earlier. I spend a day travelling to have such a meeting, and it takes me a day to return to Ottawa. If I want to leave Port au Choix and go to Cape St. George, I have to spend another nine hours driving there.
The Government has not attempted in this Bill-and 1 suggest that the previous administration, of which I was a Member, did not attempt it hard enough-to come to grips with the reality of Canada where 25 million people are spread

October 1, 1985
Representation Act, 1985
across the second biggest nation on the face of the earth. If citizenship and if service from Government and from Members of Parliament are to have some degree of equality, no matter where one lives, we in Parliament have to begin to address the nature of Canada. The nature of Canada is not only Vancouver, Calgary, Toronto, Montreal and Halifax. Our primary producers do not live in those centres. The people who make their living off the land and from the sea, the people who have dirt under their fingernails, do not live in those centres. God bless the people who do. We in the rural areas envy the amenities which have been provided to them. We as parliamentarians have to do our homework and to take another look at Bill C-74. We have to reach out in all ways and do everything within our power to make Canadians feel that, no matter where they live, they are part of the mainstream and their votes count. We have to make Canadians feel, no matter where they live, that their voice can be heard. We have to make them feel these things by the way we divide political boundaries or constituency boundaries, circonscription, en frangais. This is a bilingual country; I started my French last weekend. I guarantee in six months that I will talk the leg off a brass stove en fran<;ais. We have to begin the process.
I heard an Hon. Member opposite say that I cannot even speak English. That is a frequent complaint made about Newfoundlanders.

As I said a few moments ago, I plead with the Government to take another look at the Bill and to give it another shot by bringing in a Bill which recognizes the rural nature of Canada and the huge geographic land masses and how they are currently represented in the Chamber. I do not necessarily disagree with the Government that it may not be wise to proceed with a formula which will result in ever increasing numbers of Members of Parliament sitting in this Chamber after each census.
I accept the concept that if we simply let it go on ad infinitum we can eventually develop a system where we have more Members than are necessary and a cost borne by taxpayers that is not ncessary. As a Member who represents a rural riding I have quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, felt frustrated knowing that I am provided with a budget for a constituency office just like the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy), for want of a better example, who is provided with a budget for an office for his constituency which is two square miles and
he has his office in the middle of it, when my constituency is 500 square miles. I have my office in the middle of it. I have felt the frustration of knowing that my constituents do not have the same access to their Member as the constituents in Ottawa Centre because they have access to only one office. They might as well be going to Montreal as to try to come to my office to see me from the tip of the great northern peninsula. I have felt the frustration quite frankly of knowing that I have x number of dollars to travel within my riding.
They could hear you for 500 miles.

That's right, I have to speak loudly so they can hear me, echo off the northern lights. An urban Member has basically the same kinds of provisions to do his work. If we are not going to make the changes in the House of Commons within the formula provided under Members' services to recognize the disparity in requirements between an urban and a rural Member, then certainly we have to make changes within the provisions of the Electoral Act contained in Bill C-74 to recognize the geographic differences in the ridings in this country.
I urge the Government, because I think its Members are well intentioned to this point, to go back, to have another look, to seek advice from the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead who smiles and nods his head with compassion and understanding-
And leaves.

-and to do the right thing. Mr. Speaker, I can tell by looking at you and I know from your long years in this place and your distinguished record of integrity and compassion and understanding for we poor, young, inexperienced, rural MPs that you have an appreciation for what I am trying to say today. I recommend to the Government House Leader that he confer not only with the Speaker but confer with the Secretary of State for External Affairs and listen to the modest words of wisdom, the plea of desperation spoken on behalf of the people in the large geographic areas and rural areas of this country.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Any questions for the humble Hon. Member for Humber-Port-au-Port-St. Barbe (Mr. Tobin)? Any questions or comments?
The Hon. Member is so articulate I think if he is ever defeated from this House he could be a good vacuum cleaner salesman.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Are there any other questions or comments? Debate.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. The question before us is Bill C-74 which has to do with the representation of the Canadian people in the House of Commons. The proposal of certain safeguards is designed not to recognize the growth of population in some parts of Canada or the shifts in population which have taken place through the past decade and which were reflected in the 1981 census. It
October 1, 1985

seems to me that the proposal the Government has put before us is pretty clearly a depression proposal. It reflects quite obviously the concern of the Government to avoid expenditure and to undertake desperate measures in order to achieve that.
I am reminded of events of something over a half century ago in the Province of British Columbia, which is one of the provinces which will suffer from the proposal the Government puts forward, which were very much like this. A poor Conservative Premier named Simon Fraser Tolmie was staggering under the burden of Depression problems and he felt sufficiently desperate that he was prepared to consider the advice of a collection of Vancouver businessmen who would tell him how to solve the problems of the province. When this collection of businessmen reported, they had all kinds of drastic measures for balancing the province's budget, as they were convinced in those early days of the 1930s that the very source of the evils under which the people of British Columbia suffered was a budget in deficit. They did not appreciate that it was the falling revenues, on the one hand, resulting from Depression circumstances and the increased costs that produced this deficit situation. They felt that if they could only balance the budget they would save the people of the province.
The Tolmie Government, so convinced of the truth of these principles, which have never been heard of again, listened to this commission of Vancouver businessmen who had proposals for balancing the budget. Those proposals included drastic measures in the educational system of the province including drastic action against the University of British Columbia. For our purposes this afternoon the really interesting proposal was the one to reduce drastically the size of the provincial legislature and see one particular area of expenditure by the provincial Government reduced markedly.
It is a very similar Depression mentality based on similarly primitive economic thinking that the Government has brought before us. We heard this morning from the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Hnatyshyn) a number of arguments for the proposal and I must say in a fairly skillful way-new Members of the House always listen with interest to see what tricks we might learn for passing things off in later years-he had a number of arguments in support of the proposal. One of them was an argument for a more accountable Government and Parliament.
That particular proposition strikes me as quite contradictory to the reality with which the Government has faced us. How it is possible to slow down the legitimate growth or expected growth of the House of Commons and achieve a more accountable House I fail to understand. How it is possible to prevent the people of Canada in the natural increase that occurs and the shifts, the movements of people across the country, how it is possible to force more of them, if you will, to talk to a Member of Parliament and yet achieve a Government that is more accountable, is hare-brained reasoning. It is the kind of argument that this Government will want, I suppose, given 211 Members, numbers it hardly know what to do with in the House, and the conviction it can do anything it likes, and in those circumstances it surely is not necessary for it to add to
Representation Act, 1985
the number of Members of the House of Commons. There are more than adequate to do the job.
I would not bet on that.

As I said, based on the desire to economize, it seems quite contradictory for the Government to suggest that it is going to economize in the area of adding to the number of Members of the House of Commons and consequently hold down somewhat the growth of the salary bill and expense accounts and so on, make savings in those areas and yet begin this new regime by sweeping away millions of dollars spent over the last few years in carrying out the work of redistribution, the work of boundaries commissions, work which was in a state that could have been accepted by the Parliament of Canada quite readily without very much more effort, and obviously without a great deal of expense. That sort of waste by a Government that is anxious about savings strikes me as a second contradiction in what the President of the Privy Council put before us this morning.
Another argument was that to increase our numbers will somehow make it more difficult for Members to participate. Although coming to this House for the first time last fall with a knowledge of the opportunities for participation that Members have had in years past, opportunities to speak at real length on topics, 1 must say the Standing Orders of the House which restrict one to 20 minutes for most of us private Members on both sides of the House seem to me already a real restriction on participation. There has in fact been a proposal before us which we have accepted and upon which the Government has acted through the new Standing Orders under which Bills will be considered in legislative committees. I am sure Members will have plenty of opportunity to participate. The growth of the House by a dozen Members rather than six would not in fact represent a significant infringement on the opportunities to participate given the way in which the rules of the House presently operate. It seems to me that the argument put before us this morning were contradictory to reality. We have every reason to look very carefully at what the Government is proposing.
It seems to me that with the majority this Government holds and with the conviction that because of the choice of the people, it has the right to do anything it wants, we could end up in highly undesirable circumstances. On our side of the House, we have been pointing out a variety of failures of commission and omission on the part of the Government. I would suggest that the same is true of this Bill.
What I find curious about the way in which this Bill has been debated today is the silence from government Members regarding the proposals in this Bill. One of the features of this Bill, on the face of it, is the doing away with the well established recognition of the Province of Quebec. I am surprised that a Government with so many Members from that province has allowed itself to make this particular proposal in the legislation.

October 1, 1985
Representation Act, 1985
I must also say that this deflation of representation which the Government is putting before us affecting the Province of Alberta and to a lesser extent the Provinces of British Columbia and Ontario should have aroused other Members to protest. I realize, Mr. Speaker, that you, as a Member from the Province of Alberta, are constrained from saying anything. However, I would expect that in private, it would be possible for you to put a little pressure on Members to debate this issue.
As a Member living far from the Province of Alberta, I could, of course, wonder if there is a particular slyness involved in this proposal, the assumption being that after the 1991 Census, it will become clear that the numbers from 1981 would not have justified representation because of the migration from the Province of Alberta that has occurred over the last several years. However, that is a rather sly and insidious notion which I should hesitate to mention since I am trying to create a context of concern for the people of each province of Canada. It seems to me that when Members of Parliament from the provinces of Alberta and Quebec sit silently and let the Government carry on with these proposals to deflate the expected growth of the House of Commons, something quite insidious is going on.
In fact, this action is a revision of the Constitution Act, one of the basic documents of the country. It is a document which created parliamentary monarchy which is based fundamentally upon the will of the people as expressed in the election of Members who serve in the House of Commons. To think that that Constitution can be changed in these insidious ways without arousing Members from all the provinces of Canada is a sorry reflection on the state the Government has reached since September 4, 1984. There is much more reason for concern than has been reflected in today's debate.
In considering the particular problems that will arise if this Bill becomes law, I would like to deal quite particularly with the "province" of northern Ontario. I should, of course, for our friends in the Hansard office, put quotation marks around the word "province", although those who recognize Canadian realities realized many years ago that the only appropriate way to deal with the geographic and demographic realities of this country would in fact have been to recognize a province of northern Ontario. Since there is no such province in the Constitution of this country, the operations of Bill C-74 need to be considered very carefully by all of us who are Members of Parliament from northern Ontario.
We have already heard some representation of the difficulties that arise from the present anomalies in sizes of ridings. Before the last redistribution, northern Ontario had 12 ridings. After the last redistribution, that number was reduced by one. The question that will surely arise when the new formula is worked out for the Province of Ontario is what its effect might be on northern Ontario. According to this Bill, Ontario will only get two more seats while there has been very significant growth in population in various areas like Ottawa and Metro Toronto. In fact, there are inequities in representation there
and that will create pressures which we in northern Ontario will do our very best to resist.
The challenges to representation that now exist in northern Ontario ought not to be exacerbated in any way. To have only two more seats to deal with all of those difficulties while the population has grown so much in southern Ontario creates a very great pressure on us in northern Ontario. Particularly in northwestern Ontario, the difficulties involved in providing service to constituents, something which is surely fundamental in fulfilling the functions of a Member of Parliament, are very great. I recognize, of course, that my colleagues from the Metro Toronto area have 100,000 or perhaps even 200,000 constituents-
More.

Or more. I heard the figure mentioned before. The Hon. Member really does not need to remind me. There will be some deflation in those realities as well given the Bill before us. However, those Members are still able, without long-distance telephone charges and without unusual amounts of travelling to provide for their constituents. Compared to that, I am inclined to single out the provincial riding of Lake Nipigon because of the incredible problems I see faced by my provincial colleague. The provincial House has 125 seats. One would think that that would make it possible to avoid difficulties. However, the riding of Lake Nipigon which begins about halfway across the north shore of Lake Superior and wraps around the City of Thunder Bay some distance to the southwest is a riding that is very large. The MLA can get to most of the communities he serves only by road. Of course there are northern areas into which he can fly but that requires chartered flights in most cases. The MLA finds himself spending hours and even days on the road simply in order to be able to meet with his constituents in various areas.
I mentioned that particular challenge as a way of indicating that in my own Schedule III riding of Thunder Bay-Nipigon, I face challenges not quite as severe, but a change in distribution along the lines that this Bill suggests would certainly move me in the direction of the challenges faced by the provincial Member for Lake Nipigon. I find myself with communities to which it takes four hours to drive. I leave at 9.30 in the morning, spend some time at a meeting and some time en route and I arrive home at 10.30 that night, as I did just a week ago when I visited one of the small Indian communities. That is a community to which I do not believe I could fly. I have not investigated a charter but I do not think I could fly there. If I wanted to take the train into some of these communities on the northern CN line, Armstrong and Collins on the one side, Ferland and Mud River on the other, around to Auden and through Aroland and Nakina-and I have carefully examined the schedules-I find that a train that goes in one direction is matched by a return train three days later. Using that particular form of land transportation hardly provides for any reasonable form of travel, and that is a line on which there is no matching road at all. A number of those
October 1, 1985

places are located on lakes or rivers so there is a possibility of flying in but no one is going to tell me that getting to those sites is going to save the people of Canada any money. No one can tell me that there are not costs for the people of Canada involved in extending the size of these ridings. One can take the subway in Toronto and be anywhere one wants to be in Metro and there are streetcars, buses and so on at a quite reasonable cost. However, the expense of serving these northern areas is something which should be kept in mind at a time when we have a Government with a Depression mentality, and which is only concerned about saving costs in a number of areas.
Recognizing that it is access to the Member of Parliament and it is the Member's service to each of his constituents which is a fundamental principle of a democratic Government, I suggest that the proposal put before us by the Government slights those principles. In the desperate pursuit of some saving of money, the Government is prepared to violate time-honoured principles in distribution of representation of the House of Commons, particulrly in the Province of Quebec. I have assailed Members of the Government for their silence on this. It is quite incredible that we have had all of this put before us, a few Members of the governing Party having spoken, and the battle being left to us in the opposition who recognize the challenges which can result from what the Government has put before us, which is an enormous mistake.

Mr. Speaker, I have a brief comment and a question which I would like to raise with the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp). The Hon. Member and I represent two Ontario constituencies. I have in the past travelled on a number of occasions to the area represented by the Hon. Member and can relate to the provincial riding of Lake Nipigon which he describes and which was so well represented for a number of years in the legislature by Jack Stokes. The constituency in question, we were told by the Hon. Member, was larger than the country of West Germany and was being served in the legislative assembly of the province by one person. At the federal level, many of the constituencies are even larger than that. I wonder if I could come back to a point I raised earlier. I must preface my remarks by saying I am not trying to put any words in anyone's mouth. I am trying to elicit information and obtain constructive suggestions as to how to reorganize this whole system of electoral redistribution.
I wonder if the Hon. Member could give me his views as to whether he could see some sort of a formula which would use the land mass as a basic criteria, at least for certain regions of the country, such as exist, as I understand it, in the Province of Ontario for its electoral redistributions. I wonder if the Hon. Member would like to comment on that?

My thanks to my colleague for a challenging question. I am not going to be able to provide him with any formula in any neat way, although I understand that the work done by the provincial legislature, through commissions to establish arrangements, have led in
Representation Act, 1985
fact to a very complex formula. I realize also that there are dangers in exaggerating representation of land as such. Our system of Government is based on representation of people. However, the key principle linking these two is surely that need for access to the Member to which I referred at the end of my speech, and it is in that context that there must be some recognition of the distances Members face in reaching their constituents, and even more-given the fact that our constituents do not have the travel budgets and funds we have-their difficulty in getting to us. That is a reality which needs to be respected.
We have tried, I suppose over the years, to do that to some extent by being conservative in the representation of areas which were not growing proportionate to the country or to the new regions, and being realistic in recognizing the population growth which was occurring there. What this legislation fails to do is to deal realistically with growth while still, of course, honouring the principle of maintaining or, at least, not decreasing what exists in areas where population is more stable or, conceivably, even falling in relative terms. I think it is a sound principle and democratic for Government to ensure that constituents, in terms of access to their Members, are given some leeway in the arrangement of distribution.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Are there are any other questions or comments? Debate.

Mr. Speaker, I want to use the few minutes remaining to say that I was on the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections and the Committee on Election Expenses from 1968 to 1974. We went through then what we are going through now with respect to the matter of reconciling the principle of representation by population and taking into account our geography and where our people live. This is a non-partisan debate because it affects all Hon. Members and all Parties. Therefore, where I might part company with some of my own colleagues and my own caucus, so be it. I will be parting company with some Hon. Members in the other Parties as well. An Hon. Member who represents an urban riding with 100,000 voters within 50 square miles can keep in touch with his constituents as easy, if not easier, that the Hon. Member who has 50,000 voters within 50,000 square miles. That is what we tried to resolve in 1968, 1969, 1970 and 1971.
In my province we had 25 Members of Parliament with one million people. Then we had 21 Members of Parliament, then 17, then 13, then back up to 14, which is supposed to be the minimum. We have smaller representation with the same population to accommodate the parts of the country which have a larger population. We still have to continue to reconcile the principle of representation by population and at the same time we must take into account where the heck our people live and how accessible they are to their Member of Parliament. If they have to cover a riding of 50,000 square miles, it is a lot tougher than covering a riding like mine with 50 square miles and 95,000 people. That has to be taken into account by all Members. This country does not just consist of downtown

Toronto or southwestern Ontario. It has to take into account whatever we deal with here, every region and every part of the country.
The principle of representation by population is not disagreed with by any other Member of this House, but over the last 15 or 20 years this House has succeeded in reaching some reasonable representation for those with large populations in small ridings and those with small populations in large geor-graphical areas. Surely, in a country like this, we can do no less than continue with that. I do not agree that we should increase this House to 350 or 400 Members. Where the hell are you going to put them?
