subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   MISSING CHILDREN SEARCH ACT SUGGESTED MEASURE TO ENACT
PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   MISSING CHILDREN SEARCH ACT SUGGESTED MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
that Bill C-230, an Act to require assistance in the search of missing children, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as indicated in the motion before the House, I have presented a Bill, the short title of which is the Missing Children Search Act. I will deal with the content of the legislation in a moment. Before I do so, I want to explain
in broad terms my purpose in presenting this Bill relating to missing children to the House of Commons for consideration.
For many years those engaged in the administration of justice-police officers, prosecuting officers, social workers and the employees of the provinces and the federal authority who are concerned with justice in Canada-have been faced with the problem of missing children. More important, the problem has had to be faced by the parents and families of those missing children. It is in those interest of the parents and families that I ask the House to give consideration to this matter. While it is a matter of great interest to those responsible for the administration of justice, and while there are a great many technicalities involved in legislation that might be designed to protect children and assist in the search for missing children, we have to put aside those technicalities when we consider the plight of the parents and the families who are the victims of this social situation involving missing children. I want Members to remember that as they consider this Bill. We are not concerned with the mere technicality of the legisative provisions before us. We are concerned with the problem that is presented to Canadian society by missing children. I underline that because I want Members to know that it is not just my idea to do something about missing children. The public has the same idea. An organiation called Victims of Violence wrote to all Members Parliament in January of this year outlining the plight of missing children. I want to read part of the letter. It begins:
As parents of murdered children, we are deeply concerned with the lack of a good system in Canada to track, and hopefully find missing children.
Firstly, policies must be changed at local levels as far as officially considering a child missing. Usually, since most missing children do show up within a number of hours, police do not respond to missing children reports with the seriousness they do with a missing car.
Without blaming the police across this nation and without condemning anybody involved in the administration of justice, a fact of life in the administration of our penal laws is that a missing child does not receive the same attention as a missing car. Parliament surely has to do something about that. I ask Parliament to consider this legislation that I presented because of that fact. It has been stated by a parent of a missing child. It goes on to say, just to underline the point-as if it needed underlining-that if you were to ask the police in Canada for a list of missing children they would not have one, but if you ask them for a list of missing motor vehicles or recreational vessels, they would have such a list. That is the horrible situation in which we in Canada find ourselves.
I want to again refer to some literature on the subject of missing children. I came across an article in a periodical, Teaching Today, which was sent to all teachers in the Province of Alberta. This is from the spring 1985 issue. The author of the article, Aaron Bushkowsky, states that the slowness of local law enforcement authorities with respect to investigation of missing children cases is disheartening. He states, and 1 want to make this point very clearly:
-to be missing is not a crime:
Because being missing is not a crime, the police are often excluded from the process and procedure involved in the
October 1, 1985

search for missing children. That is exactly what this Bill is designed to deal with. Let me very briefly outline the provisions of the Bill which I have introduced.
What it does is define a missing child. It simply says that a child under the age of 16 whose whereabouts is unknown to his or her parent is a missing child. It is as simple as that. When a child is missing, the parent under this legislaiton has the right to execute a warrant which is then given to any police officer in Canada. The police officer is then required to commence a search for the child. I am sure the representative of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) if he has an opportunity to speak on this Bill, will say that this Bill creates difficulties with respect to jurisdiction between the Parliament of Canada and the legislatures of the provinces of Canada. I certainly admit that that is a problem. I have attempted to overcome that problem by declaring that the missing child procedure as outlined in the Act is to be part of the criminal law of Canada. Clearly the Parliament of Canada has the right and authority to legislate with respect to criminal law. Whether that disposes of the argument I am not prepared to say except that it is the best attempt that I can construct. I want to return to the real heart of the problem which is the missing children across Canada.
Statistics are lean. Inquiries have been made. The Ministry of the Solicitor General of the Province of Ontario had a missing children project and it attempted to compile some statistics. The indication was that approximately 1,081 children are still missing in Canada. That does not include the thousands and thousands of cases involving missing children which are resolved quickly or over a period of time. In the United States it is considered to be an even greater problem with literally thousands and thousands of cases being reported. I have an article here which indicates that no one is sure of the exact numbers but it is estimated that 1.5 million children are missing from their homes each year. The report indicates that many or most of them are returned but some of them end up as victims of abuse or victims of homicide.
If the Parliament of Canada cannot act to at least provide some method or process to deal with the problems, then we are shirking our responsibility to the people of Canada, in particular to the parents and families of missing children. We want to find a viable method that can assist in resolving the problem. Nothing is perfect. Let me depart from that point by saying that so often in the House of Commons and legislatures across the country we abandon any hope of taking action for fear that our action may not be as effective as it could be. In other words, we do not make a start. Missing children is an area in which we have not made a start. At some point we must put some legislation on the statute books which at least recognizes that there is a problem under the laws of Canada and the provinces with respect to missing children.
I do not want to reflect badly on the police, but the problem is that missing children do not fit into our framework of criminal law. The extent to which they fit into the framework
Missing Children Search Act
of child protection laws is lacking in effectiveness. Child protection laws are affected by provincial boundaries which are difficult to cross in search of a missing child. In some cases it is even difficult to cross municipal boundaries in search of a missing child because quite often child protection agencies are confined to a municipal territory. It has been demonstrated time and again that there must be a national vehicle for dealing with missing children.
The second point which gives rise to legal difficulty with respect to missing children is the characterization of that state. If a 15-year old simply wants to escape the wrath of a person in the home, or for some almost legitimate reason wants to leave home, we must consider whether the child is not entitled to protection outside the home. Consequently, in that kind of a situation, the police authorities are unwilling to become involved and often the child protection authorities act without haste. We get confused in terms of trying to characterize the case. Once you recognize that there are almost legitimate cases of missing children, you tend to colour all the reported cases with that possibility and give the benefit of the doubt and some police agencies and other persons engaged in the administration of justice prefer to take no action. The result is that nothing happens and the missing child is then endangered by being subjected to harmful treatment or even, in some cases, homicide.
We are trying to characterize the cases of missing children which should be assisted by the legal process. That is the first task of this or any Bill which purports to deal with missing children. The second task is to provide a process which will allow a search for missing children and for the return of them to their proper homes. The fact that this Bill may not accomplish that and that some more perfect means can be imagined is not an excuse for not making a start.
I do not want to take all of the time which is available to me because I know there are other Members who want to speak on this Bill. However, I should not leave this subject without referring to the fact that there has been a great deal done by various organizations which are concerned about the subject of missing children. A program called Adam, which was aired in the United States on NBC Television and subsequently in Canada, brought a great deal of national attention in the United States and in Canada to the subject of missing children. It also brought attention to organizations such as Child Find and its programs. There is an organization called the National Centre for Missing and Exploited Children which regularly publishes pictures and identifying material concerning missing children. In many cases, this has resulted in the lost child being found, often in very difficult circumstances.
I do not want to imply that there are not a great many Canadians and other people across North America vitally concerned with this matter and who have taken steps to resolve it by forming organizations in the hope of getting all of the people who are interested in the problem together. I would like to emphasize the fact that most of this work is being carried on by volunteers in our society. That does not excuse Government from taking a specific interest in the matter and seeking

October 1, 1985
Missing Children Search Act
techniques, processes, and procedures that will assist at Government levels in resolving this problem.
I would like to end my remarks by repeating that my motivation for bringing this matter before Parliament is to get recognition of the fact that missing children are a problem in Canadian society. We have seen heinous crimes involving missing children. We have seen difficulties experienced by families of missing children. I have responded to this problem by formulating Bill C-230, the Missing Children Search Act. That is only to demonstrate that it is possible to have legislation. 1 am sure that there are greater legal minds than mine which can formulate more effective legislation. I hope that those minds will be put to work on this subject rather than having it merely swept away and forgotten to become another musty record of the House of Commons. I appeal to all Members of the House of Commons to take into account the concern that has been and will be expressed with respect to missing children. Let us make a start.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   MISSING CHILDREN SEARCH ACT SUGGESTED MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the Hon. Member for having brought Bill C-230 to the attention of the House. It is a very important subject indeed when we consider that over 1,200 children over the age of 10 are known to be missing. There are 160 children under the age of 10 who we know are missing in this country as we speak right now. In any given year 2,000 children are reported missing. This happens as a result of many things. Some children leave the home, some are abducted by strangers, and some are abducted by family. It is with regard to the latter that I want to make my remarks this afternoon.
On October 13, 1982 a child by the name of Tina Lynn Malette was abducted. At the time the child was in my daughter's class at school. She was abducted by her natural father who, for all intents and purposes, had never seen the child. The father had only lived in this country for a short period of time. He came from another country, abducted the child, and took her to Tunisia. To this day we are still looking for a way to bring the child back to this country. We have found out where the child is and the mother can speak to her by telephone, but we are not able to return her to this country. I have asked for the assistance of the Right Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) and I believe that he has done all that he can. However, unfortunately, there are no extradiction treaties between Canada and Tunisia and we are, therefore, powerless to do anything.
The father was never married to the mother and never lived with her for any length of time. For all intents and purposes, he was a complete stranger to that child before the date of the abduction. Since this man is the father of the child, Tunisian authorities claim to have sufficient legal grounds to allow her to stay there. They claim that they have no authority to deport the child. Of course, this is the daughter of a citizen and therefore the child is a citizen as well, even though she never lived with the father, does not bear his name and the father does not even have a birth certificate which attributes him with the paternity of that child. Nevertheless, the child is there.
On several occasions I have attempted to do what I could about this situation. In July, 1983, I wrote a letter to a Member of Parliament from Tunisia whom I met at a parliamentary conference and who purported at the time to be interested in the case. He never responded. In December, 1983, I wrote again to that same Tunisian Member of Parliament about the same issue but the letter was never answered.
I wrote on two other occasions to the leader of the only political party, as I understand it, in that country. Those letters were never answered either. It was only this year, once I became a federal Member of Parliament and raised the issue in the House that we could at least get some reaction from the Tunisian authorities. At that time the Tunisian Ambassador finally said that there was nothing he could do about the case. It is strange that if they thought they were so right in their actions that they would find it so difficult to express it publicly before.
Be that as it may, after writing to the Tunisian Ambassador in December, 1984 and February, 1985, we managed to get some form of a statement from the Ambassador in April or May of this year when he expressed the position of his country which I have already enunciated.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs tells us that the only way to bring this child back to Canada is to launch legal proceedings in the courts of Tunisia. A number of people whom I know have started a Tina Lynn Malette trust fund. A number of prominent people from the Ottawa-Carleton area are trustees of this particular fund. We have begun to raise the money necessary to hopefully launch a successful legal campaign in order to return the child to Canada.
As a father of two children, with one child who was in the same class as this particular girl, one really discovers how powerless each one of us is if someone wants to come to our home and take our child away to another country or even a different province in certain cases. Even if that man was the natural father of the child-because he was otherwise a total stranger, not even in possession of a birth certificate or anything else acknowledging the paternity, much less a passport or visa-what would be the difference if someone came to my house and took away my child who was the same age, her best friend and in the same class at school? I suggest the situation would be almost identical.
If it was my child who was over there, what would I do to bring her back? I would probably do the same as the mother of Tina Lynn Malette and cry a lot and try hard without success to this point. I do not believe that all those officials with whom I have dealt on this issue had anything else but good intentions. Certainly, the Right Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs and his precedessor as well as others have made a legitimate effort to assist me and, of course, my constituent in bringing this child back. However, we have not had any success as yet. I commend any Member of the House who attempts to work in such a way as to enhance the chances of bringing lost children home.
October 1, 1985

The situation that I have described is somewhat different than the one brought to our attention by the Hon. Member who proposed the Bill, but it is another example of lost children in this country and how each one of us, as parents, are really powerless and helpless when these things happen. We always think that it happens to someone else, but this incident happened so closely to me that I really believe I would be totally powerless. I am sure when Members think about it seriously, they will see that we are powerless in such cases.
I tabled a petition in the House earlier this year, consisting of some 7,000 names of Canadians who are concerned about the case of Tina Lynn Malette and wanting a resolution to the problem, urging the Government of Tunisia to bring her back. Of course, it still claims that under its law it is not possible.
It is my hope that the legal action that has begun will be successful. I cannot wait for the day when we will go to Mirabel Airport and hopefully take the child off the plane. However, it is bound to be a while yet. Certainly I, and I am sure my colleagues, intend to allow this Bill to pass. It is a good Bill with good intentions.

Member for Halifax West but they were given by the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell. I believe it is necessary to have more detailed facts on the number of missing children to determine the number missing as a result of a family situation, a non-family situation or whether it is a poor family home situation where the child seems to have run away.
I attempted to find those facts in the Badgley Commission but there is not much information with respect to the problem of using the police power to return missing children as proposed by the Hon. Member in his Bill.
I certainly agree with the Hon. Member that it must be a terrible experience to be a parent of a missing child. As I listened to the speech by the Hon. Member for Halifax West, it appeared that there is a grass roots movement to deal with
Missing Children Search Act
this problem as often happens in Canadian society. Members will recall the group called MADD. These were people against impaired drivers. They campaigned for tougher penalties because some of their family members had been victims of impaired drivers. They began to pressure Members of Parliament. They were not represented by any funded group, business or labour body. They were ordinary Canadians who were concerned about this problem.
Members of Parliament did receive a letter from a group called The Victims of Violence and I thank them for writing to us. We appreciate the kind of grass roots nature of this group. I will come back to that in a minute.

Is this an amendment to the Criminal Code or not? I think it should be, and it should not stand as a separate Bill. If it becomes an amendment to the Criminal Code, there are certain aspects of the Bill we should look at very closely. We have to balance our concern against missing children and the ability to do something in terms of an investigation and in getting the children back.
Some of the wording in his Bill is not crystal clear. I know he said that this was a general approach to flag he issue and to keep pressure on so that something will be done. In Clause 7 there can be a search warrant to search premises and so on when people suspect a missing child is involved. This goes a little far, and there are some civil liberties concerns here. Do we want to give the police that kind of power? Can that kind of power be abused? We have to weigh that against the concern of getting the bureacracy, and I include the police, to pay more concern to missing children as opposed to missing cars and boats.

speechtext:
The organization made the statement. It is a serious allegation, Mr. Speaker. We are more concerned about property than we are about people. We are more concerned about missing cars and boats than about missing kids. If that is true, it is something we have to change.
The Hon. Member said that 1.5 million children went missing each year in the United States. That is an awful lot of children. We could do well when this Bill gets into committee to debate why that situation is happening. Is it because our victims, in a sense runaways, are a product of home abuse? Are they taken away by another parent because of marriage breakdown and the difficulties associated with that? Are they abducted by the Clifford Olsons of this world because of crime in our society? It would be good to have a breakdown of those figures.
We need to look at the cause of the situation. Is it racism in the United States in terms of black families? Is it poverty? There is certainly a lot of poverty in the United States and in Canada. That should be investigated when we consider the Bill in committee.
I can tell the Hon. Member that there are different ways of dealing with-and I don't think they are mutually exclusive- missing children. One is enforcement; putting some fire under the police in a procedural legal way to search out and take serious reports of missing children. Another way is to deal with the matter in a preventive state so children never go missing in the first place.
In my province of British Columbia, the Government has cut back family services. It has cut back services to children. It has cut back on the number of social workers and on abuse centres. We should be looking at those as preventive measures. If we can ensure strong families, ensure that people do not live in poverty and ensure that there is no family abuse, then things at the other end will change and we will have fewer missing children.
I have to point out that this is a Government prepared to cut back on family allowances while spending a billion dollars to bail out a bank. If the Government cuts back on family allowances, it will guarantee more family problems because income is being cut back to families that really need it. You cannot have it both ways, Mr. Speaker.
The Badgley Report of which I spoke listed a number of preventive measures. It suggested minimum standards of service be set up for the police and for the social workers. The report talked about sexual abuse cases. In this context, the same could be said generally about missing children. A way of reporting to the police, getting the information to other provinces and agencies, ways of making people aware should be approached. It was suggested we have an office of a commissioner for children which would bring some of these departments together. These are useful suggestions. I think the Hon. Member and I agree that what he was reflecting today is the general grass roots feeling saying that bureaucracy is not doing enough, the police are not doing enough, and it is of real concern that no one is listening and we are frustrated. These are real problems and they must be listened to.
There is alienation and frustration in our society which is reflected in problems like missing children. I know some of it is inevitable and it has always been with us. It seems in our materialistic society that there are more breakdowns and less stability in the family and in society. This is reflected in prostitution where the frustrated in a less caring society find they must resort to prostitutes. It is reflected in children running away and in the crazies in the streets, the Olsons of this world, who murder children. It is reflected in all sorts of ways. That is the negative aspect to society. On the positive side the Hon. Member has taken the time to bring this Bill forward. He is responding to a grass roots situation. 1 have some concerns about the wording of the Bill, the civil liberties aspects and the way it fits in with the Criminal Code. Also I have some concerns about whether it would really be effective. However, I say to the Hon. Member that it is an initiative well worth looking into.
I will take my seat now and hope that the Bill will pass into committee today so that we can discuss the matter further.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to say a few words in support of Bill C-230, standing in the name of the Hon. Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby), an Act to require assistance in the search for missing children. As he has indicated, the propose of the Bill is to make it possible for the parents or persons responsible for a child who is missing to obtain assistance to locate that child in Canada. Human and other resources are part of the administration of justice and should be made available for that purpose. Of course the purpose of the Bill is to try to make them available.
I am particularly interested in supporting it because of my own personal experience with a friend, Mrs. Inge Cant, who has gone through a terrifying experience of a similar nature with her own child. Mrs. Cant separated from her husband in about 1981. They had one child. They fought a very bitterly contested custody battle. She received custody from the courts. Her husband appealed and received access to the child on weekends. On one of those weekends, he and the child, Jonathan, disappeared. Mrs. Cant then spent 20 months trying to find her son, Jonathan. Not only did she spend that length of time, but she spent a lot of her own money. Mr. Speaker, you may have read about this case in the newspapers. I should like to quote from an article which appeared in The Toronto Star, on February 16, 1984. In part, it reads:
With painstaking accuracy, Inge Cant has kept accounts.
From the $100 long distance telephone bills, to the $20,000 legal bills, the search for her abducted son, Jonathan, cost more than most people could afford.
October 1, 1985

Certainly more than Cant, a legal secretary who made about $20,000 a year, could ever hope to pay for on her own.
But from the day Jonathan was taken from Cant's estranged husband ... the search was on. In total, it cost Cant, her family and friends more than $100,000.
That $100,000 was spent as follows-$40,000 for private detectives at $35 per hour, $20,000 in legal fees and other expenses for long distance telephone calls, travel and accommodations. Finally, her search took her to Australia; after 20 months she located her son in that country.
She took with her to Australia a police officer who kindly agreed to accompany her. She paid all the expenses of that police officer to go with her to Australia to try to bring back the child. Once they had boarded the airplane with the child, Australian police got on and took her and the child off the airplane, because the estranged husband had obtained a court order to fight for custody in that country. She had to go through the custody struggle all over again.
Finally, she is back here in Canada with her son, Jonathan. However, the estranged father, who went to Australia on a stolen passport, still has it. She lives in terror that everything will happen again. As I said, it cost here some $100,000 to find her child. That is the type of problem which the Bill tries to address and tries to find a logical solution for.
Just this afternoon I talked with the Deputy Chief of Metropolitan Toronto, Jim Clark, about this problem. He told me that in the last 10 years in Metropolitan Toronto there have been 64,000 reports of missing children and that that figure did not include those abducted by their parents. Of that figure, six have remained missing for a period of over one year. Also he said that from 35 to 70 cases involving missing children are outstanding in Toronto at any one time.
The Hon. Member for Halifax West referred to a number of voluntary organizations which are interested in and try to assist with this problem. Child Find is one to which my hon. friend referred. It takes the fingerprints of children and tries to use them for assistance. There is the Child Photo Program which takes photographs of children, and of course there are the block parent programs which try to keep an eye on children in neighbourhoods. All these organizations are helpful, but it is a sad commentary, as other Hon. Members have said, that it has to be done by volunteers and that the Government is not involved in the program. It is high time the Government became involved.
Also Deputy Chief Clark of Metropolitan Toronto said that the United States had a federally funded program called the National Centre for Missing and Exploited Children. It coordinates information on missing children. We do not have such an organization in Canada. Our police departments are linked by computer and they have to try to search out information via computer when they obtain a report on a missing child. Unfortunately they cannot necessarily access the computer information of all other police departments. The present system is ineffective in dealing with the problem. We need something like a national centre for missing children. It may well tie in with the program under the divorce legislation as well as the maintenance and custody legislation currently
Missing Children Search Act
before the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. Perhaps that information system can be used to assist in these situations.
The Hon. Member brought forward another excellent suggestion as to how this matter should be dealt with. In one way or another, I believe that the matter has to be dealt with quickly by Parliament. We should refer the Bill to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs today so that we can get on with solving the problem.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   MISSING CHILDREN SEARCH ACT SUGGESTED MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin by congratulating the Hon. Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) on bringing forward Bill C-230. I assure him and all Hon. Members in the House that the Liberal Party supports the Bill in principle. We in Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition would like to see the subject matter referred to either a legislative committee, especially set up to deal with the subject matter, or to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, so that we can look into the entire question of missing children. The Hon. Member made an excellent submission. I assure him of our full support in having the subject matter dealt with as expeditiously as possible.
I need not articulate the pain and anguish which parents suffer as a result of their children who go missing. If there is anything that we as parliamentarians can do to try to assist those parents in finding their children, I think we will have served this subject matter well. The fact remains that nationally we are not doing what we can to assist parents. The Hon. Member for Halifax West has introduced a particular Bill which will address the problem in a particular fashion. As other Hon. Members have indicated, as of January, 1984, a total of 1,224 children between the ages of 10 years and 16 years went missing in Canada. An additional 160 child under the age of nine years were also missing. In total, over 2,000 children are reported missing each year. The Canadian Police Information Centre usually has an accurate record of the number of children missing but not the circumstances of their disappearance. Some police departments across the country may enter incomplete descriptions or conflicting information. As the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) pointed out, missing children fall into three categories-runaways, stranger abductions and parental abductions. Contrary to popular belief most police departments do not wait a prescribed period of time, for example 24 hours, before recording a child as missing. They treat each case individually, taking into consideration factors such as whether the child is known to be a runaway or there are feuding parents where parental abduction is likely.
As other Members have indicated, corporations are eager to get involved in searches for missing children. There are more than a dozen corporations who want to put their names and dollars into any program involving missing children. So we have the private sector that is quite prepared to get involved in this particular area, to try to assist in whatever way possible. What we need is a federal Government initiative. We all know
7234

October 1, 1985
Missing Children Search Act
that there is no Canadian legislation dealing specifically with missing children.
In the U.S., as has been pointed out, the Missing Children Act was signed into law in October of 1984. It provides a $4 million fund administered by the Department of Justice to co-ordinate the work of volunteer groups and help them establish toll-free telephone lines and information clearing houses. I think the Government of Canada should look at that particular legislation as a model and as a basis to develop our own procedures to deal with missing children. The United States also requires Attorneys General in each state to allow parents access to police computer systems to ensure that their missing children's names have been entered and if not to find out why not. In this regard it is important to note that RCMP officers and officials of Statistics Canada have not kept national statistics on missing children since 1976 because of conflicting reporting methods. This is another subject matter that ought to be considered by the appropriate committee.
The Liberal Party as well as, I am sure, all Hon. Members in this House are extremely concerned with respect to the problem of missing children. Last February Mr. McGuigan, an Ontario Liberal Member of Parliament, released the results of his three-month study on missing children. He concluded that police departments lack the resources to conduct proper investigations, that Governments have been slow to pass legislation to protect children and that there is a low level of public awareness of this particular problem. His report is an important contribution to the literature that we already have on this particular subject. Mr. McGuigan debunks many of the myths concerning missing children. Some of his conclusions are that most children who run away do so because of intolerable conditions at home, not because they are searching for fun and adventure as some would argue. They are often fleeing from physical, emotional or sexual abuse.
While about 95 per cent of missing children are runaways, an increasing number are victims of abduction. Few children abducted by strangers are recovered alive. The abductors include pedophiles, pornographers, black market baby peddlers or psychotics. He says "Child prostitution, sexual and physical abuse, mental anguish and torment and even death await many of these children in such unfortunate circumstances".
There are an increasing number of cases involving the abduction of children by parents, usually after a divorce or a custody battle. The McGuigan Report said that the main motive is revenge against the other parent, not love for the child. It is a mistake to assume that children abducted by parents are in no real danger. Organizations which are concerned with such children have reported that the majority of them were either beaten, molested or neglected.
Mr. McGuigan also noted in his report that there were 22 children murdered in Canada last year and that children frequently are the victims of serial murderers such as by Clifford Olson in British Columbia and by U.S. mass killer Henry Lee Lucas.
Mr. Speaker, may I take this opportunity to applaud the efforts of Mr. McGuigan on that in-depth study in which he
was involved. He indicated that he plans to introduce a resolution in the legislature in Ontario asking for a full scale inquiry into the problem of missing children and hopes that this inquiry will be conducted by the Legislature's Social Development Committee.
Among some of the recommendations in the McGuigan Report is that a province-wide and eventually nation-wide registry of missing children should be established. I think that is an excellent suggestion and something that Parliament can address and can do so quickly. He also noted that police forces are hampered in their investigations by the lack of an up-to-date central data base. Once again, the federal Government can assist with respect to an up-to-date data base to ensure that as much information as possible is available to parents and others, including police departments in the search for missing children.
It is important to note that most abducted Canadian children are taken to the United States, where provincial custody orders are not always enforced. The McGuigan Report stressed that there has to be a broader international agreement to respect foreign court orders. I call on the Government of Canada to address the problem of parents who abduct their children and take them to foreign jurisdictions, especially to the United States. I should point out that several nations have signed an international agreement called the Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction which binds the signatories to help return missing children within their boundaries. France, Portugal, Switzerland, Ontario and several other Canadian provinces have ratified the agreement. Britain and the United States have signed it but have yet to ratify it.
In conclusion I would urge all Hon. Members in this House to support this particular Bill in principle and to refer the whole subject matter of missing children to a parliamentary committee to ensure that whatever can be done is done by this Parliament to assist those who have searched in vain to find missing children. I think it will be a tremendous step forward and a credit to each and every Member of this House.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for giving me the opportunity to speak on this most worthwhile proposal.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING-ROLE OF CHARTERED BANKS. (B) EXPENDITURES OF TAXPAYERS' MONEY
BANKS AND BANKING-ROLE OF CHARTERED BANKS. (B) EXPENDITURES OF TAXPAYERS' MONEY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on another occasion during the Adjournment Debate I stressed my agreement with the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDou-gall) when she spoke of the importance of confidence to the health and stability of our Financial institutions. I pointed out that when Opposition Members ask questions in the House, it is not out of a desire to undermine confidence or create doubts or uncertainty; on the contrary, it is because we have a responsibility as Members of Parliament to assure ourselves and the taxpayers that the decisions made by the Government are sound, reasoned, considered and based on full and complete information.
Since the Government First announced its intention to bail out the Canadian Commercial Bank on March 25 we have tried repeatedly but with limited success, to assure ourselves of the Government's care in examining all the information before committing large sums of taxpayers' money.
We in the Official Opposition supported the Government in the original rescue operation because, although we were not given a full account of what had occurred, we expected to get one when the matter reached committee stage. We also believed that the Government's statements about the Canadian Commercial Bank's viability were based on fact and analysis.
The Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs was in fact given relatively narrow terms of reference when it came to study the CCB issue. We were operating under significant time restraints and for various reasons much of the information requested by the committee was not provided. We were not much better informed after the committee's examinations than we were before. This is why, when the CCB's closing was announced on Labour Day, we came back into the House asking many of the same questions we had been asking all along, questions to which we still do not have full answers.
We know enough from what has been said in the House and from what has been said by players in the financial and banking community to be sure that the Government's many assurances about the effectiveness of the bail-out and the viability of the CCB were not, as we had believed, based on knowledge of the facts. I have not counted the number of times the Minister of State for Finance has said that she acted on the best information available at the time. She has said it often but she has never told us just what that information was.
We know that the decision to bail out the CCB was reached without a full assessment of the bank's loan portfolio. Some of the banks taking part in the bail-out offered to provide expert staff to conduct a complete audit over the weekend the negotiations were taking place. We know that this offer was refused, and that instead the unprecedented decision to use taxpayers' money to bail out a bank was taken with only partial analysis of the bank's loan portfolio and, furthermore, that the CCB itself decided what segment of its loan portfolio was made available to the bail-out group.

October 1, 1985
Adjournment Debate
The Minister had access to the reports of the external auditors of the CCB but she has not given any assurance that this information was used in the decision-making process. It seems as though there was information available that the Government did not use when it decided to bail out the CCB, and since we are not getting any specific answers about what information was used, we must conclude that last March the Government took an enormous and unwarranted leap of faith.
Not until mid-July did the Government set about finding out just what it had got itself into, and not until mid-August when the results came in did the Government know what little basis there was to believe the bail-out would have saved the CCB. This is an error of truly mind-boggling proportions.
We have had an attempted bail-out which resulted in the failure of two banks, and which will cost the taxpayers of this country up to $1 billion. We have seen the Government bail out a bank, then liquidate that bank and another. Shortly we will be debating the legislation to reimburse uninsured depositors in those institutions, and those who made the decisions that are now costing taxpayers SI billion are refusing to provide information to this House and refusing to give straight answers to the questions that we as responsible Members of the Opposition have been asking.
The establishment of a commission of inquiry, as announced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), takes the matter outside of Parliament. While the commission may be a useful and valuable exercise, it does not answer for the fact that the Government and its Ministers are accountable to Parliament for their decisions and actions and that so far they have not seemed willing to satisfy the House that they have acted properly.

It has also been suggested that one or another of the chartered banks offered to provide personnel in sufficient numbers to have carried out a more complete examination and that the Government declined such offers.
It is the case, however, that an independent review of certain of the assets was made by a team drawn from a number of the participating banks, working under the direction of an official of the office of the Inspector General of Banks. During the
week of March 18, assets booked in both Edmonton and California were reviewed. In the course of discussions with the participating banks, the question of asset values naturally received a great deal of attention.
Accordingly, on Friday, March 22, arrangements were made to have credit officers of some of the participating banks review a sample of the loans to be included in the support arrangements. That work was carried out on Sunday, March 24, by 10 or 11 bankers at the two locations. As mentioned, those officers devoted their attention to the loans identified by the bank as being unsatisfactory.
Following the completion of the support arrangment, two bankers were appointed as special representatives of the Inspector General of Banks as required by the agreement. Over a period of several weeks those individuals reviewed all of the accounts included in the support arrangement.
As the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) has said more than once, the decision to proceed with the support package was based upon the best information available at the time. Of necessity, in the circumstances, that information was primarily prepared by the bank but it was subjected to a degree of independent review by experienced bankers. The support group of banks offered to participate in a review. The offer was accepted by the other participants, including the CCB itself, and a group of bankers was made available for the prupose. All participants recognized, however, that the final decision and announcement had to be ready for the opening of business on Monday, March 25, 1985.

First of all, Mr. Speaker, a note should be made that no one was laughing and that nothing whatsoever was taken in jest. If the Hon. Member would like to try and tailor his remarks to the question he put, he might do an awfully lot better. The question has nothing to do with banks, and in fact this question First arose before there was any collapse of any bank. Considering that the Hon. Member did not know what he was talking about, although he comes from an area in which this product grows, it is rather unfortunate that he was not better prepared.
I am pleased to elaborate on the answer that was provided to the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall) on March 21 regarding the hypothetical imposition of a tariff on Canadian blueberries entering the European Economic Community.
As the Hon. Member pointed out last March, the ECC had officially notified GATT of its intention to retaliate against quotas that the Canadian Government imposed on imports of beef and veal when we invoked the Meat Import Act on
Adjournment Debate
January 1, 1985. The European Economic Community threatened to impose a 25 per cent tariff on imports of Canadian blueberries. The tariff was supposed to go into effect on April 15 and last until the end of the year. Retaliatory actions were also threatened against our exports of beef, veal and pork offals, natural honey, mustard seed and flour, maple syrup, rye whiskey, feeds and unmanufactured, unstemmed tobacco.
The European Economic Community is our leading customer for blueberry exports. In recent years the European market has accounted for nearly 60 per cent of our blueberry exports worth an average of $15.5 million per year. Last year our exports gained strongly, thanks in part to the lower value of the Canadian dollar compared to the U.S. dollar, the absence of tariff barriers, and a strong market development effort by Canadian producers in co-operation with the federal Government.
I should explain that under GATT rules Canada has the right to take action restricting beef and veal imports, but adversely affected trading partners, such as the EEC, also have the right to retaliate if it is not possible to negotiate a mutually agreed upon solution. Mr. Speaker, officials from the Department of External Affairs have, in fact, negotiated an equitable solution to this problem and the blueberries were not affected.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to raise the issue of pornography in the House of Commons once again. I am sure that every Member of Parliament agrees that this is one issue which must be kept on the top of the agenda. This House has an obligation to give as much attention as possible to this matter until significant progress can be made in arresting the harm that is being inflicted on our children, our families, and our society.
There are not very many issues which enjoy such a broad base of support as does the opposition to pornography. Everyone recognizes that pornography is a bad influence on those who are directly involved. As well, I think everyone would agree that even those who choose not to involve themselves, including most of society, are in many ways hurt by it. Many innocent young people, and indeed Canadians of all ages, become victims of those depraved individuals who feed on the warped moral values depicted through the pornography industry.
People who buy pornography, and people who become wealthy in promoting it, do so with the justification that they are not hurting anyone. Who are they kidding? It is very clear in speaking to police, doctors, and social agencies, that this industry is claiming more victims with each passing day. People who buy pornography, first and foremost, hurt themselves. It is quite clear that it draws people into a vortex of dependency and addiction leading to increasingly more difficult tastes to satisfy and to a host of related personal problems. More importantly, the person who buys pornography contributes to the health of a vast and growing industry.

October I, 1985
Adjournment Debate
This industry does not exist without supporting a great many undesirable industries, including drugs, prostitution, crime, and the exploitation of women and children.
Finally, those who say that pornography does not hurt anyone are ignoring the effect it has on a community where it is permitted in plain sight in the local variety stores, and now in the shops that rent videos for home use. Our children begin to take it for granted when they see adults making use of such material. Do we want the children of our country to consider such trash as the norm? Absolutely not.
The political and social traditions of our country have overwhelmingly supported our community's proper role in defending itself from the creeping social disintegration that is, in a continuous cycle, both a result and a cause of pornography, and a direct attack on the family unit which I believe is the foundation stone of our country.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) has indicated that the Government will present a package of legislation to deal with pornography some time around Christmas. The Government will, to some extent, anchor this legislation on the recommendations of the Fraser Report on Pornography and Prostitution.
The Fraser Report presents a very sophisticated analysis of the problem, but there was a strong suggestion of tolerance toward the pornography that is not of the most offensive quality-that is explicitly violent, or featuring children. In fact, the report recommended that if pornographic material does not reflect these two themes, then it should be freely available if it is marked clearly and only sold to adults over 18. This is totally unacceptable.
Most Canadians do not want pornography in their corner stores, and most do not want to encounter it at all. There is absolutely nothing good or of redeeming value about pornography. So if some people do want it, let us not make it easily accessible.
Because of the increasing flood of pornography on the market today, I believe the time has come for Parliament to deal with its removal in a decisive and forthright manner. Too often in the past, our legislators have been handcuffed by a definition of pornography that is at the same time narrow and vague. Too often material has been defended because it might not be associated with some overt violence, or because it has some transparent claims of artistic merit. Only if the Government provides a broad and sweeping definition of pornography will significant gains occur in reducing this problem.
I believe the stiffest penlaties should be reserved for material exploiting children, or displaying violence. The publishers, wholesalers and retailers of these materials must be held accountable through our courts.
At the same time, let us never for one moment show the slightest tolerance for other forms of pornography. I hope the Government will show the decisive leadership that is necessary to reverse the alarming trends that have been developing. A good example is reflected by the adolescent-oriented material
we see daily on television that is obscene in every sense other than the graphic depiction of obscenities. This process can only start with the Canadian people clearly stating, through the Government in Parliament, that pornography in our society is both undesirable and unacceptable. I believe it is our responsibility as legislators to provide the necessary laws to protect our children, not only from the harm inflicted by those individuals who absorb pornography, but more important, from the gradual destruction of their collective sense of moral standards. The future of Canada, above all, depends on the healthy and mature attitudes of our younger generation. I urge the Government to act on this before it is too late.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that my hon. colleague has brought this topic up for a more detailed reply than can be given during Question Period. Of course, 1 am happy to see that so many Members of the House here tonight who want to be informed further on this subject.
Recent years have seen a dramatic upsurge in the availability of sexually explicit material, a significant diversification of form of that material such as paperback books, comic books, movies, video tapes, so-called marital aids and other paraphernalia and an ever extending system of distribution of the material.
In 1981, the Ministers of Justice and National Health and Welfare created the Committee on Sexual Offences Against Children and Youths, known as the Badgley Committee. The report was submitted on August 22, 1984. It contains recommendations for amendments to the Criminal Code to prohibit the use of a person under the age of 18 years in the making of ponorgraphy and to prohibit the possession and distribution of such material. Further, it recommends that the sale of pornographic materials to persons under 16 should be a criminal offence and that measures should be adopted to improve the investigation and enforcement of these offences. These recommendations are being reviewed by the Department of Justice.
On June 23, 1983, the Minister of Justice announced the creation of a special committee to study pornography and prostitution, under the chairmanship of Mr. Paul Fraser, Q.C. of Vancouver. The committee held a series of public hearings in 20 cities across Canada. The interest generated by the work of the committee was apparent at the public hearings, where there was very active participation of both organized groups and concerned citizens. The Department of Justice conducted a program of empirical research for the committee. This program included: a national population survey on the attitudes and views of Canadians concerning the control of pornography; a comprehensive review of the literature on the impact of pornography; experimental studies on the effects of pornography, and several other related studies of areas not covered by existing research findings.
The report of the Special Committee on Pornography and Prostitution, the Fraser Committee, was tabled in the House of Commons on April 23, 1985.
October 1, 1985

The proposals of the Fraser Committee with regard to pornography would fundamentally alter the present Criminal Code provisions on obscenity. Mere possession of certain clearly defined pornographic materials, most notably child pornography, would be a criminal offence. The distribution or sale of materials falling within a category of "sexually violent and degrading pornography" would be proscribed unless the material could be shown to have educational or scientific purpose or artistic merit. All other sexually explicit materials would be required to be enclosed in a wrapper and clearly labelled so those who wish could avoid exposure to such materials. Sale of all types of pornography to those under 18 would be prohibited.
The recommendations of the Fraser Committee are now under review by officials in the Department of Justice, and following a period of consultation with provincial Governments and private sector groups, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Cros-bie) will announce the Government's response to those recommendations and those of the Badgley committee.
